## Abstract

`jmjax` samples joint longitudinal-survival models with NUTS/HMC and, on
identical data, mixes substantially better than `JMbayes2`'s block-Gibbs/
Metropolis sampler - most robustly, and independently of any optional
reparameterization, on the association parameter a joint-model analysis is
usually run to estimate, where the advantage is several-fold to an order of
magnitude (Sections 6.3, 7.1, 8). This document does six things. First, it names the mechanism precisely: a location degeneracy
between subject-constant fixed effects and the matching linear combination
of correlated random effects, which the likelihood pins only through their
*sum*. This is not specific to the random intercept - this document shows,
and traces to source, that the same degeneracy recurs for the random
*slope* on time, independently of how many other covariates are in the
model. Second, it describes `jmjax`'s fix (`control$orthogonalize_b0` /
`orthogonalize_b`), a NUTS-space reparameterization that removes the
absorbable directions from the random-effect prior rather than imposing an
exact constraint, and explains concretely why it is a different (and, on
current evidence, better-behaved) approach than an earlier, already-retracted
attempt at the same problem (`wishart_gibbs_centered`). Third, it gives the
fix a formal treatment: a precise definition of the absorbable set, an
exact characterization of it, and a proof that the construction removes
only genuinely absorbable directions - so that the model is provably, not
just empirically, unchanged. The same analysis shows the construction is
*not* complete: because it inspects one design column at a time while the
absorbable set depends only on the column space, a spline or
orthogonal-polynomial longitudinal mean paired with a random slope defeats
it silently, and a basis-independent replacement is given - and now ships.
Fourth, it settles the question the first draft left open, and the answer
is two-sided. Posterior calibration *fails* for the reparameterized
coordinates: credible intervals for exactly the swept parameters come back
too narrow by close to the predicted $\sigma_b/\sqrt{N}$, reproducing the
failure mode that retracted `wishart_gibbs_centered`, while point
estimates stay unbiased - which is precisely why a bias check would have
passed it. But the damage is to the *coordinates*, not the target, and it
is exactly removable: a closed-form, unit-Jacobian affine map carries the
reparameterized draws back onto the identified ones, using quantities the
same fit already stores and requiring no refit. The correction is proved
exact for the likelihood, shown to differ from the unconstrained posterior
only by an explicit prior-invariance weight that is negligible under any
diffuse prior on $\beta$, and measured to restore both coverage and
interval width. Fifth, it
reports a replicated simulation study across a covariate-count sweep (k = 1, 4, 8, 12
extra covariates) and an independent real-data check (the `aids` clinical
trial data, never used to build any of the diagnostics below), both showing
the same pattern: the *swept-coefficient* efficiency advantage over
`JMbayes2` is large, statistically significant, and *does not grow with
covariate count* - because its dominant source is the covariate-count-
independent slope degeneracy, not the covariate-count-dependent one. A
separate, k-dependent effect is `JMbayes2`'s own catastrophic loss of
convergence on its random-effects covariance parameter as covariate count
grows (max R-hat past 10,000 at k = 12), which inflates naive "jmjax vs
JMbayes2" ratios for reasons that have nothing to do with `jmjax`'s
reparameterization. Sixth - and this changes the document's central claim -
it measures the effective sample size of the corrected estimand itself,
`beta_corrected` in Section 4.9's terms, and finds that the large advantage
just described for the *swept* coordinate does not transfer to it: a pilot
measurement puts the reportable estimand's gain at roughly 1.25x-1.31x, not
an order of magnitude. Read together with a direct, reparameterization-
independent measurement of the *association parameter* `alpha` - the
quantity a joint-model analysis is usually run to estimate - the picture
that emerges is a reallocation of `jmjax`'s central claim, not a loss of
it: a default, non-orthogonalized fit already beats `JMbayes2` on `alpha`'s
own ESS/second by 2.44x on real data and 5.7x-8.1x in simulation, with the
reparameterization option contributing little on top (roughly 1.0x-1.5x,
inconsistently across the two datasets). The large, robust, well-evidenced
advantage is therefore Layer 1 - `jmjax`'s generic NUTS/HMC engine against
`JMbayes2`'s block sampler (Section 8.1), now demonstrated directly rather
than only argued for - and it needs no reparameterization option to hold.
`orthogonalize_b0`/`orthogonalize_b` remains a genuine, worthwhile
contribution on its own, narrower terms: it diagnoses and fixes a real
identifiability bug that silently miscalibrates credible intervals for
swept coefficients (Section 9.1), exactly as an earlier, retracted attempt
at the same problem did, with a closed-form, verified correction - but its
efficiency benefit for the coefficients it targets, once measured on
coordinates a user may actually report, is modest, not dramatic. A late
follow-up (Section 9.1.2), added after the claim above was set, finds
that a further, currently experimental reparameterization
(`orthogonalize_b0_rotate`) recovers most of `beta_corrected`'s missing
efficiency - roughly 5x-8x over a default fit across three small pilots
and two baseline-hazard forms - while leaving calibration unchanged
within Monte Carlo noise on the one design checked so far. It is reported
for completeness, because the evidence is consistent across every
configuration tried, not because it has yet received the breadth of
validation (multiple designs, real data, the random-slope column) the
rest of this document's claims have. Section 4.10 proves the construction exact, shows that a conditioning
effect of NUTS's diagonal mass matrix is sufficient to explain its gain
without the funnel-type pathology first suspected, and derives an extension to the
random-slope column that remains to be implemented and tested. The document closes by connecting
this to established reparameterization and MCMC literature, including the
specific point (Geyer, 1992) that explains why a sampled coordinate can
mix beautifully while the linear combination needed to recover the
identified quantity does not.

## 1. Motivation

Across every real and simulated dataset `jmjax` has been benchmarked on, its
NUTS/HMC sampler mixes better than `JMbayes2`'s sampler - sometimes by a
modest, explainable margin (Section 7, and the existing benchmark section of
`vignette("jmjax-validation")`), sometimes by a striking one. The striking
cases concentrate on regression parameters, are essentially unaffected by
whether `JMbayes2`'s *own* diagnostics have converged, and get *more*
striking, not less, as the number of covariates grows - but, as this
document shows, for a more specific and more interesting reason than "more
covariates favor gradient-based samplers" in general.

This is worth writing up carefully rather than reporting only the headline
ratios, for two reasons. First, the mechanism is real, reproducible, and -
as far as a genuine literature search turned up - not previously documented
in exactly this form (Section 2.6), which makes it worth a citable record
rather than only inline code comments. Second, an honest accounting has to
separate what is actually attributable to `jmjax`'s design (a targeted
reparameterization of a diagnosed degeneracy) from what is actually
attributable to `JMbayes2`'s degradation under conditions its sampler was
not designed to be robust to (Section 8). Conflating the two would overstate
`jmjax`'s novelty on the axis where the advantage is smallest (nuisance
parameters) and understate the well-grounded, citable case for it on the
axis where the advantage is largest (regression parameters).

## 2. Background: reparameterization in hierarchical Bayesian models

### 2.1 Centered and non-centered parameterizations

The general problem of how a hierarchical model's *parameterization* -
independent of its likelihood - determines whether a given MCMC sampler
mixes well is the subject of a substantial literature going back at least to
Papaspiliopoulos & Roberts (2003), "Non-Centered Parameterisations for
Hierarchical Models and Data Augmentation," in *Bayesian Statistics 7*
(Bernardo et al., eds., Oxford University Press), and formalized in
Papaspiliopoulos, Roberts & Sköld (2007), "A General Framework for the
Parametrization of Hierarchical Models," *Statistical Science*, 22(1),
59-73 (also arXiv:0708.3797). Their central point, restated for this
setting: whether a hierarchical parameter should be sampled in its "centered"
form (as the quantity of direct scientific interest) or a "non-centered"
form (as a standardized deviation from a mean, with the mean itself a
separate parameter) is not a matter of taste - it changes which directions
of the posterior a given sampler can move efficiently along, and the right
choice depends on how informative the data are relative to the prior for
that parameter.

### 2.2 Why this bites gradient-based samplers specifically

Betancourt & Girolami (2013), "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical
Models" (arXiv:1312.0906), and Betancourt (2017), "A Conceptual
Introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo" (arXiv:1701.02434), give the
geometric account of *why* a poor parameterization specifically hurts
Hamiltonian/NUTS samplers: HMC's efficiency depends on a roughly uniform
curvature (so a single, global step size and mass matrix work everywhere),
and a degenerate or near-degenerate direction in the posterior - a ridge, or
a funnel - forces the sampler either to take very small steps (to stay
stable along the narrow direction) or to fail to move efficiently along the
wide one. Hoffman & Gelman (2014), "The No-U-Turn Sampler," *Journal of
Machine Learning Research*, 15, 1593-1623, is the reference for NUTS itself
and documents the same general sensitivity to posterior geometry that
motivates adaptive path-length selection in the first place.

**Neal's funnel is a different pathology and should not be conflated with
this one.** The canonical hard case for HMC in hierarchical models, due to
Neal (2003), "Slice Sampling," *Annals of Statistics*, 31(3), 705-767, is a
*curvature* problem: a hierarchical variance parameter changes the scale of
the parameters below it, so the posterior narrows sharply in one region and
widens in another, and no single step size handles both. The location
degeneracy this document is about is not a curvature problem - the
posterior's curvature along the degenerate direction is essentially flat
(it is informed only by a prior, not sharpened or narrowed by the
likelihood at all). Both problems are usefully addressed by
reparameterization, and both are discussed together in introductions to HMC
for exactly that reason, but they are mechanistically distinct and the fix
for one is not automatically evidence for, or against, the other.

### 2.3 A directly analogous, already-quantified example

Stan's own User's Guide, in its "Collinearity" / redundant-intercepts
discussion of "Problematic Posteriors," works through almost exactly the
degeneracy this document is about: a model with two intercept parameters
whose likelihood is invariant to adding a constant to one and subtracting it
from the other, so only their *sum* is identified. Stan's documented,
measured comparison (100 data points, standard normal) across three
versions of that model is close enough to `jmjax`'s own case to quote
directly:

| Model | Mean leapfrog steps | ESS/sec | R-hat |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Non-identified (flat prior on both intercepts) | ~1,400 | ~200 | 5.2 (non-convergent) |
| Weakly identified (both intercepts given a `normal(0, 10)` prior) | ~150 | ~1,900 | 1.0 |
| Identified (single intercept) | ~3 | ~31,000 | 1.0 |

The "weakly identified" row is the mechanistically exact analogue of
`jmjax`'s default (non-orthogonalized) fit: `jmjax` does not leave `beta_0`
and `mean(b_i0)` entirely unconstrained (that would be improper), it
constrains their *split* only through the prior on the random effects, at
scale `sigma_b0/sqrt(N)` - a weak, N-dependent identifying prior in
precisely the sense of Stan's middle row. Reading the ratios off that row
relative to the fully identified one - roughly 50x more leapfrog steps and
roughly 16x lower ESS/sec from the *weak-prior* case alone, before even
reaching the fully non-identified case - is a useful, independently-sourced
sanity check on the magnitude of what a location degeneracy costs, prior to
any numbers specific to `jmjax` below.

### 2.4 The other side: why block/conditional samplers are specifically vulnerable

Roberts & Sahu (1997), "Updating Schemes, Correlation Structure, Blocking
and Parameterization for the Gibbs Sampler," *Journal of the Royal
Statistical Society, Series B*, 59(2), 291-317, is the classical reference
for the complementary fact this document needs for Section 8: a Gibbs
sampler that updates parameters in blocks (as `JMbayes2`'s does - it
combines Metropolis-within-Gibbs updates for regression coefficients with a
closed-form conditional update for the random-effects covariance) degrades
specifically as the *correlation between blocks* grows, because each block
is updated conditional on the current value of the others and can only move
as fast as that conditional distribution allows. This is a distinct
mechanism from the location degeneracy itself: it does not require an
unidentified direction, only a strongly correlated one, and it predicts
degradation that tracks *inter-block correlation growing with problem size*
even in a model that is *fully* identified everywhere - which is exactly
the shape of the `JMbayes2` covariance-collapse finding in Section 6.4.

### 2.5 Applied precedent

Ogle et al. (2020), "Ensuring Identifiability in Hierarchical Mixed Effects
Bayesian Models," *Ecological Applications*, 30(7), e02159, documents the
same class of problem (fixed effects and random effects competing to
explain the same variation) arising in applied hierarchical models outside
the joint-modeling literature, and is useful as evidence that this is a
recognized, recurring failure mode across the wider Bayesian hierarchical-
modeling literature rather than an artifact specific to joint models.

### 2.6 What appears to be genuinely new here

A deliberately honest gap: no prior work was found that documents this
*exact* instance - a random-slope-mean-vs-fixed-slope-coefficient aliasing,
in a *joint* longitudinal-survival model, empirically shown to explain a
*widening* efficiency disadvantage for a competing block-sampler
implementation as covariate count grows, with the covariate-count-
independence of the underlying mechanism itself confirmed against the
sampler's own source code. The pieces above (non-centered reparameterization
theory, HMC's specific sensitivity to it, Gibbs samplers' specific
sensitivity to growing correlation) are all separately well established;
their combination and application to this specific model class, with this
specific empirical signature, is offered here as this document's actual
contribution - not a rediscovery of general theory.

### 2.7 A related point this document needed later: ESS is a property of the functional, not the sampler

Geyer (1992), "Practical Markov Chain Monte Carlo," *Statistical Science*,
7(4), 473-483, is the classical reference for a fact that becomes
load-bearing in Section 9: effective sample size and Monte Carlo standard
error are defined with respect to a *specific scalar function* of the
chain being averaged, not as a property of the sampler or the state vector
in the abstract. Two different linear functionals of the same joint draws
- say, a sampled coordinate, and a different linear combination of that
coordinate with another block entirely - can therefore have arbitrarily
different effective sample sizes even though they come from the identical
run. This is not a surprising or unusual fact in the MCMC literature; it
is why Section 9.1.1's correction needed its own, separate ESS measurement
rather than inheriting the swept coordinate's.

## 3. The location degeneracy in jmjax's joint model

### 3.1 Setup

`jmjax`'s longitudinal submodel, for the random-intercept-and-slope case
(`random_effects = "intercept_slope"`, `q = 2`) that this document is
concerned with, is

$$y_{ij} = \beta^\top x_{ij} + b_{i0} + b_{i1} t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}$$

with `beta` the fixed-effects vector (including an intercept and any
baseline covariates), `b_i = (b_{i0}, b_{i1})` subject-level random effects
with a correlated Normal prior, and `t_ij` the time of observation `j` for
subject `i`. The survival submodel links to this through `alpha` and the
usual functional forms; nothing below changes as a function of the survival
side, so it is suppressed in this section's notation.

### 3.2 The intercept-level degeneracy (established prior to this document)

If `x_ij` contains an intercept column (or, more generally, any column that
is constant within subject `i`), a shift `b_{i0} -> b_{i0} + s_i` for a
subject-constant `s_i` changes nothing about the fitted mean as long as
`beta` absorbs the matching shift on that column - the likelihood
constrains only the **sum**, not the individual split. This was already
diagnosed and documented (`vignette("jmjax-validation")`, "The experimental
`wishart_gibbs_centered` option"; see also the `orthogonalize_b0`
documentation in `?jm_fit`) prior to the work in this document, via a
measured `corr(beta_0, mean(b_i0)) ~= -0.95` on real data and the resulting
poor `beta_0` mixing.

**An earlier attempted fix, and why it was retracted.**
`control$random_effects_method = "wishart_gibbs_centered"` addressed this
by constraining the random intercepts to sum to exactly zero at *every*
posterior draw - a hard, exact Gibbs-sampler constraint. It worked, in the
narrow sense of improving `beta_0`'s mixing (`beta_0` ESS improved roughly
4.8x in its own validation). But further validation at a larger sample size
found it introduces a genuine, quantitatively characterized **credible-
interval miscalibration** for `beta_0`: point estimates stayed unbiased, but
the reported posterior standard deviation did not fully reflect the true
uncertainty, because the exact constraint removes real finite-sample
variability in the sample mean of the true random intercepts that `beta_0`
must otherwise absorb. It is documented in the package as exploratory only,
not recommended for final inference. This episode matters for what follows
in two ways: it establishes that this general class of problem is not
solved just by "removing" the degeneracy by any means available, and it is
the point of comparison Section 3.5 returns to.

### 3.3 The new finding this document adds: the same degeneracy recurs for the random slope, independently of covariate count

The session behind this document set out to characterize how `jmjax`'s
efficiency advantage over `JMbayes2` scales with the number of covariates
`k`, on the hypothesis (reasonable a priori, and the initial motivating
observation) that more covariates create more room for `beta_0`-type
degeneracies and so a larger advantage for the orthogonalized fit. A fast
`n = 500`, `k in {1, 3}` readout initially seemed to support this - but it
was a single seed per cell, and the much larger, replicated sweep in
Section 6 overturns it: the regression-parameter advantage of full
orthogonalization (`orthogonalize_b`, "arm E" below) over the default fit
("arm A") is **flat across k = 1, 4, 8, 12** (roughly 11-15x throughout, no
trend - Table 6.3), not growing with covariate count as first guessed.

The explanation, verified directly against `jmjax`'s own source
(`inst/python/jmjax_backend/mcmc_model.py`, the `_absorbable_basis`
function), is that the *dominant* win from full orthogonalization is not
the `k`-dependent, `beta_0`-type degeneracy at all. It is a **second,
separate degeneracy between the fixed slope coefficient `beta_1` (the
population-average coefficient on `time`) and the population *mean* of the
random slopes, `mean(b_i1)`** - and this one is present as soon as there is
*any* random slope on time, regardless of how many other covariates are in
the model. `_absorbable_basis`'s own docstring states this plainly, in code
that is data-driven (it does not hard-code which columns are absorbable; it
discovers them from the actual design matrices at fit time):

> "For q = 1 (a random slope on time) it picks up `time` itself, giving the
> sum-to-zero constraint on b_1, and would also pick up any
> covariate-by-time interaction present in X."

That is: whenever the fixed-effects design includes a `time` column (as any
model with a fixed slope on time does) and there is a correlated random
slope on time, the fixed slope and the mean random slope are aliased in
exactly the same "sum is identified, split is not" sense as the intercept
case - and this holds at `k = 0` extra covariates just as much as at
`k = 12`. This was directly confirmed by the replicated log in Section 6:
across every `k` tested, the *binding* (lowest-ESS) regression parameter
under the default fit is consistently `beta_1`, never one of the `k`
covariate coefficients themselves - and `orthogonalize_b` (which sweeps the
slope column too; `orthogonalize_b0` does not) is what fixes it, cleanly and
consistently, at every `k`.

### 3.4 The fix: `orthogonalize_b0` / `orthogonalize_b`

`control$orthogonalize_b0` (intercept column only) and `control$orthogonalize_b`
(every random-effect column, i.e. intercept and slope) implement a NUTS-space
reparameterization rather than an exact Gibbs constraint. For each
random-effect column `q`, `_absorbable_basis()` inspects the actual (not
assumed) fixed-effects design `X` and random-effects design `Z` and
constructs an orthonormal basis `Q` for exactly the subject-level directions
that some fixed-effects column can reproduce - i.e. the directions a shift
in `b[:, q]` could equivalently be expressed as a shift in `beta`. The
sampled random-effect column is then replaced by its residual off that
column space (its projection onto the orthogonal complement of `Q`), so the
degenerate directions are simply never given to the sampler as free
parameters in the first place; everything the likelihood cannot separately
identify about that direction is left entirely to `beta`, exactly as it
should be.

**The model is unchanged.** Every direction swept out of a random-effect
column lies in a column space `beta` already spans, so for any posterior
draw there exists a shift of `beta` that reproduces identical fitted values
- the set of achievable mean structures is exactly the same before and
after. What changes is only which parameterization NUTS samples in. Section 4 proves this (Corollary 1), and Section 5 verifies it
empirically - "the algebra says so" and "the implementation does what the
algebra says" are different claims, and both are now addressed: the first
in Section 4, the second at general `k` in Section 5. Section 4 also shows
that the *converse* claim - that the construction removes every absorbable
direction - holds only under a condition on the design basis that a spline
or orthogonal-polynomial longitudinal mean violates (Section 4.5).

The option is data-driven rather than assumption-driven in a second sense
worth noting: if the design has no intercept and no column matching a
random-effect term, `_absorbable_basis` returns no basis and the option is
a documented no-op with a warning, rather than silently doing nothing or
erroring. The implementation also reports, via a `RuntimeWarning` at fit
time, exactly which basis (if any) was constructed for each column and from
which `X` columns - the log excerpts quoted in Section 6 include these
messages verbatim, which is what makes it possible to state with confidence
*which* directions were actually removed on each run, rather than inferring
it indirectly from downstream ESS numbers.

### 3.5 Previously-measured magnitude, real data

Prior to this document, `orthogonalize_b0`'s own package documentation
(`?jm_fit`) already recorded a direct measurement on the `pbc2` dataset
(n = 312, 4 chains x 1000 draws, figures reported in the space NUTS actually
samples): with an intercept and one baseline covariate in the design,

- `corr(beta_0, mean(b_i0)) = -0.9709`
- `corr(beta_2, age-slope(b_i0)) = -0.9715`
- against `+0.0543` for `beta_1` (a within-subject, non-absorbable
  contrast, included as a negative control)
- minimum ESS for the two affected coefficients alone, 441 and 526, against
  2893 and >4000 for the corresponding *identified sums* - a recoverable
  factor of **6.6x and >7.6x**.

### 3.6 Why this is not the same fix as `wishart_gibbs_centered`, and what has *not* yet been checked

Directly on the same `pbc2` data, `wishart_gibbs_centered` (which pins only
`mean(b_i0)` at exactly zero, removing one direction of the degeneracy) is
recorded as moving `beta_0`'s ESS 441 -> 1490, but `beta_2`'s ESS 526 -> 291
- *worse* than doing nothing for the second parameter, because pinning one
direction of a two-dimensional degeneracy does not remove the other.
`orthogonalize_b0`/`orthogonalize_b` differ in two structural ways: they
identify *all* absorbable directions per column from the actual design
(not just the intercept's own), and they operate as a continuous
reparameterization inside the space NUTS explores with gradients, rather
than as an exact constraint imposed by a separate Gibbs step. This is why
the fix generalizes correctly to the multi-covariate case where the earlier
one did not.

It is important to be equally direct about where the two constructions turn
out to be *alike*. `wishart_gibbs_centered`'s efficiency gain was checked
for calibration and found wanting (Section 3.2). An earlier version of this
document argued that `orthogonalize_b0`/`orthogonalize_b` had a plausible
mechanistic reason to behave differently on that axis, since they change
the prior's *support* rather than pinning a specific value the way an exact
zero-sum constraint does, and listed the check as the single most important
piece of unfinished work.

The check has now been run, and that argument was wrong: on the
reparameterized coordinates these options miscalibrate in the same way and
for the same reason (Section 9.1). What differs is the remedy. Because the
damage here is confined to the coordinates in which the sampler reports -
the likelihood is untouched, by Corollary 1 - the discarded uncertainty can
be put back exactly, in closed form, from the draws the same fit already
produced (Section 4.9). No analogous closed-form recovery exists for an
exact Gibbs constraint, which destroys the information rather than
relocating it. That is the substantive difference between the two
approaches, and it is a sharper one than the argument it replaces.

## 4. Formal correctness of the absorbable-basis construction

Section 3.4 states, informally, that `_absorbable_basis` removes exactly
the directions the fixed effects can absorb, and that the model is
therefore unchanged. Section 5 checks the consequence empirically. This
section states and proves the claim, and in doing so establishes three
things the informal argument does not: a precise condition under which the
construction is sound for the *joint* model rather than the longitudinal
submodel alone (Section 4.4), a precise condition under which it is
*complete*, together with a natural design where completeness fails
(Section 4.5), and a stronger justification than uniformity for the
treatment of subjects whose longitudinal data does not determine their own
ratio (Section 4.6).

### 4.1 Notation

Index subjects by $i = 1, \dots, N$ and subject $i$'s longitudinal
observations by $j = 1, \dots, n_i$, taken at times $t_{ij}$. Write
$X_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i \times p}$ for subject $i$'s longitudinal
fixed-effects design and $Z_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i \times q}$ for its
random-effects design, and let $z_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i}$ denote the
column $Z_i[\,\cdot\,, q_\ast]$ of the particular random-effect column
$q_\ast$ under consideration (the index is suppressed from here on).
Let $b \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times q}$ collect the random effects and
$\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$ the fixed effects.

The random effects enter the joint likelihood in exactly two ways: through
the longitudinal mean

$$\mu_{ij} = x_{ij}^{\top}\beta + z_{ij}^{\top} b_i,$$

and through the shared trajectory $m_i(t) = x_i(t)^{\top}\beta +
z_i(t)^{\top} b_i$, which enters the hazard through $\alpha$ and is
evaluated at the event time $T_i$ and at the Gauss-Legendre quadrature
nodes used for the cumulative hazard. This second channel matters for what
follows and is easy to overlook: `_absorbable_basis` inspects `X_long` and
`Z_long` only, while `b` also reaches the likelihood through
`X_time_surv`/`Z_time_surv` and `X_time_quad`/`Z_time_quad`. Both of those
are built by `build_time_design()` from the *same* `long_formula` and
`random_formula`, evaluated at new time points with the subject's baseline
covariates, so each design column is a fixed function of time,
$f_j(t; c_i)$ for $X$ and $g(t; c_i)$ for the random-effect column, with
$c_i$ subject $i$'s baseline covariates.

### 4.2 What "absorbable" means

**Definition 1.** A vector $v \in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ is an *absorbable
direction* for random-effect column $q_\ast$ if there exists
$d \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$ such that, for every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the
simultaneous shift

$$b[\,\cdot\,, q_\ast] \;\leftarrow\; b[\,\cdot\,, q_\ast] + c\,v,
\qquad \beta \;\leftarrow\; \beta + c\,d$$

leaves $\mu_{ij}$ unchanged for every $(i,j)$ and $m_i(t)$ unchanged for
every $i$ and every $t \in [0, \tau]$. Write $\mathcal{A}$ for the set of
absorbable directions.

Because both shifts are linear in $c$, it suffices to check $c = 1$, and
$\mathcal{A}$ is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{N}$. Two remarks fix
the scope of the definition. First, invariance of $\mu$ and $m$ implies
invariance of the whole joint likelihood, since the likelihood depends on
$b$ only through those two quantities; the definition is therefore about
*likelihood* invariance. Second, it is emphatically not about invariance
of the prior or the posterior - the prior on $b$ is not invariant under
these shifts, and that asymmetry is the entire point of the
reparameterization. Section 4.7 returns to this.

Definition 1 splits into a longitudinal requirement,

$$X_i\,d \;=\; -\,v_i\,z_i \qquad \text{for every } i, \tag{L}$$

and a trajectory requirement,

$$x_i(t)^{\top} d \;=\; -\,v_i\, g(t; c_i)
\qquad \text{for every } i \text{ and every } t \in [0, \tau]. \tag{T}$$

### 4.3 Exact characterization

Let $\bigoplus_i \mathbb{R}^{n_i}$ denote the space of stacked
per-subject observation vectors, and define two linear maps into it:

$$\mathcal{T}: \mathbb{R}^{p} \to \bigoplus_i \mathbb{R}^{n_i},
\quad (\mathcal{T}d)_i = X_i d,
\qquad
\mathcal{U}: \mathbb{R}^{N} \to \bigoplus_i \mathbb{R}^{n_i},
\quad (\mathcal{U}v)_i = v_i z_i .$$

$\mathcal{T}$ is the map from a shift in $\beta$ to its effect on the
fitted longitudinal means; $\mathcal{U}$ is the map from a shift in the
random-effect column to its effect on the same quantity.

**Proposition 1 (characterization).** Under requirement (L) alone - that
is, for the longitudinal submodel in isolation - the set of absorbable
directions is

$$\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{long}}
= \mathcal{U}^{-1}\!\big(\operatorname{range}\mathcal{T}\big)
= \{\, v \in \mathbb{R}^{N} : \mathcal{U}v \in \operatorname{range}
\mathcal{T} \,\}.$$

*Proof.* Condition (L) says precisely that $\mathcal{T}d = -\mathcal{U}v$
for some $d$, i.e. that $-\mathcal{U}v \in \operatorname{range}
\mathcal{T}$. Since $\operatorname{range}\mathcal{T}$ is a subspace it is
closed under negation, so this holds if and only if $\mathcal{U}v \in
\operatorname{range}\mathcal{T}$. $\square$

Proposition 1 is worth stating because it makes the target of the
construction a property of the *column space* of $X$ - not of any
particular basis for it. That observation is what Section 4.5 turns on.

### 4.4 Soundness, and the condition the survival submodel imposes

`_absorbable_basis` computes, in the notation above, the index set

$$K = \{\, j : \exists\, s^{(j)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N}
\text{ with } X_i e_j = s^{(j)}_i z_i \text{ for every } i \,\}$$

- the columns of $X$ that are *individually* subject-constant multiples of
the random-effect column - and returns an orthonormal basis $Q$ of
$\operatorname{span}\{ s^{(j)} : j \in K \}$, obtained by QR with a
rank-revealing tolerance on $|\mathrm{diag}(R)|$.

**Proposition 2 (soundness, longitudinal).**
$\operatorname{span}(Q) \subseteq \mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{long}}$.

*Proof.* For $j \in K$ we have $X e_j = \mathcal{U}s^{(j)}$ by
construction, so $\mathcal{U}s^{(j)} \in \operatorname{range}\mathcal{T}$,
hence $s^{(j)} \in \mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{long}}$ by Proposition 1. Since
$\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{long}}$ is a subspace it contains the span of the
$s^{(j)}$, and $\operatorname{span}(Q)$ is that span. $\square$

Soundness for the *joint* model requires more, because the ratio test is
evaluated only on the observed grid $\{t_{ij}\}$ while requirement (T)
quantifies over all $t \in [0,\tau]$.

**Condition (S) - structural extension.** For each $j \in K$, the
grid identity $f_j(t_{ij}; c_i) = s^{(j)}_i\, g(t_{ij}; c_i)$,
$j = 1,\dots,n_i$, extends to $f_j(t; c_i) = s^{(j)}_i\, g(t; c_i)$ for
all $t \in [0,\tau]$.

**Proposition 3 (soundness, joint model).** If (S) holds, then
$\operatorname{span}(Q) \subseteq \mathcal{A}$.

*Proof.* Proposition 2 gives (L). Under (S), $x_i(t)^{\top}e_j =
f_j(t; c_i) = s^{(j)}_i g(t; c_i)$ for all $t$, so taking $d = -e_j$
satisfies (T) for the direction $s^{(j)}$; linearity extends this to the
span. $\square$

(S) is not automatic, but it holds in every case the option currently
targets: a subject-constant column has $f_j \equiv c$ and $g \equiv 1$,
a `time` column has $f_j(t) = t = 1 \cdot g(t)$, and a covariate-by-time
interaction has $f_j(t) = c_i t = c_i\, g(t)$ - all identities in $t$,
not coincidences on a grid. In general, if $f_j - s_i g$ lies in a linear
function space of dimension at most $n_i$ that is determined by its values
at $n_i$ distinct points (polynomials of degree $< n_i$, for instance),
then (S) follows from the grid identity. It can fail for subjects with few
observations relative to the dimension of the spanning basis, where the
relation may hold at the observed points by coincidence.

(S) is also *checkable* rather than merely assumable, at negligible cost:
`X_time_quad` and `Z_time_quad` are already constructed and passed to the
backend, so running the same ratio test on the quadrature grid and
confirming the same $s^{(j)}$ would verify (S) directly instead of
resting on the argument above. This is recommended in Section 4.8.

### 4.5 Completeness, and a design where it fails

Soundness says nothing is wrongly swept. Completeness - that nothing
absorbable is *missed* - is a separate claim, and it is the one that does
not hold in general.

Assume for this subsection that $z_i \neq 0$ for every $i$ (every subject
has at least one observation at which the random-effect column is
nonzero); Section 4.6 treats the remaining case. Then $\mathcal{U}$ is
injective, and Proposition 1 gives
$\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{long}} = \mathcal{U}^{-1}(\operatorname{range}
\mathcal{T} \cap \operatorname{range}\mathcal{U})$.

**Proposition 4 (completeness criterion).**
$\operatorname{span}(Q) = \mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{long}}$ if and only if

$$\operatorname{range}\mathcal{T} \cap \operatorname{range}\mathcal{U}
= \operatorname{span}\{\, X e_j : j \in K \,\}. \tag{C}$$

*Proof.* $\mathcal{U}$ is injective, so it is a bijection from
$\mathbb{R}^N$ onto $\operatorname{range}\mathcal{U}$, and it carries
$\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{long}}$ onto $\operatorname{range}\mathcal{T} \cap
\operatorname{range}\mathcal{U}$ and $\operatorname{span}(Q)$ onto
$\operatorname{span}\{X e_j : j \in K\}$. Equality of the two subspaces
upstairs is therefore equivalent to equality downstairs. The inclusion
$\subseteq$ of the right side in the left always holds, by Proposition 2.
$\square$

Condition (C) says that every vector lying in both the column space of $X$
and the image of $\mathcal{U}$ is a combination of those *individual*
columns of $X$ that lie in the image of $\mathcal{U}$. This is a
restriction on the basis, not on the model, and it can fail.

**Example 1 (completeness fails for a spline or orthogonal-polynomial
longitudinal mean).** Let every subject be observed at the same
$m \geq 3$ distinct times, let $Z = [\,1,\ t\,]$ with $q_\ast$ the slope
column, and let

$$X = [\,1,\ \ t + \tfrac{1}{2}t^{2},\ \ t^{2}\,].$$

No single column of $X$ is a subject-constant multiple of $t$: the ratios
are $1/t_{ij}$, $1 + \tfrac12 t_{ij}$ and $t_{ij}$ respectively, none
constant in $j$. So $K = \emptyset$ and the construction returns no basis
for the slope column. Yet $d = (0, 1, -\tfrac12)$ gives $Xd = t$ exactly,
so the uniform direction $v = \mathbf{1}_N$ satisfies (L) and (T), and
$\mathbf{1}_N \in \mathcal{A}$. Hence
$\operatorname{span}(Q) = \{0\} \subsetneq \mathcal{A}$.

This was confirmed directly against the shipped implementation (extracted
and run on constructed designs; `dev/verify_absorbable_basis.py`): on
$X = [1, t, x]$ the slope column correctly yields one direction from
column 1, while on the $X$ above it yields `None`, with the compensating
$\beta$ shift verified to reproduce $t$ to machine precision.

The example is not contrived. The column space in Example 1 is
$\operatorname{span}\{1, t, t^2\}$ - exactly what `y ~ poly(time, 2)` or a
natural-spline longitudinal mean produces. The raw monomial spelling
`y ~ time + I(time^2)` *is* caught, because there `time` appears as its
own column; the orthogonalized or spline basis for the very same function
space is not. By Proposition 1 the absorbable set depends only on
$\operatorname{span}(X)$, whereas the construction's answer depends on
which basis of that span `model.matrix()` happens to emit. That gap is the
precise statement of the limitation.

Its practical consequence is sharper than the generic caution in
Section 9.2. With a spline or orthogonal-polynomial longitudinal mean and a
random slope, the column-wise construction silently failed to remove the
$\beta_1 \leftrightarrow \overline{b_{i1}}$ degeneracy that Section 3.3
identifies as the *dominant* source of the efficiency advantage - and the
existing no-op warning would not fire, because the intercept column still
yields a basis (verified: in Example 1 the intercept column returns one
direction). The user would see the option accepted, a basis reported for
`b[:,0]`, and no indication that the slope column was left untreated.

There is a constructive repair, and it follows directly from
Proposition 1. Writing $P_{\mathcal{T}}$ for the orthogonal projector onto
$\operatorname{range}\mathcal{T}$,

$$\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{long}}
= \ker\!\big( (I - P_{\mathcal{T}})\,\mathcal{U} \big),$$

so the correct basis is an orthonormal basis of the null space of the
$\big(\sum_i n_i\big) \times N$ matrix $(I - P_{\mathcal{T}})\mathcal{U}$,
computable with one SVD and no loop over columns. This is basis-independent
by construction, recovers the column-wise answer whenever (C) holds, and
costs a single decomposition performed once outside the sampler.

This repair is no longer hypothetical: it ships as
`_absorbable_basis_exact()` and is the basis the implementation actually
sweeps, with the column-wise search retained alongside it for attribution
and cross-checking. Section 4.8 describes what the implementation does with
both, and Section 4.9 shows that the same generators the exact
construction produces are what make the calibration correction computable.

### 4.6 Subjects whose own data does not determine their ratio

Drop the assumption that $z_i \neq 0$. If subject $i$ has $z_i = 0$ - no
observation at which the random-effect column is nonzero, for instance a
baseline-only trajectory when $q_\ast$ is the time-slope column - then
$e_i \in \ker\mathcal{U}$, so requirement (L) places no constraint
whatever on $v_i$. Read through the longitudinal submodel alone, *any*
value of $v_i$ is absorbable, which is what the source comment at the
imputation branch asserts.

For the joint model this is not so, and the distinction matters.

**Proposition 5.** Suppose $v \in \mathcal{A}$ with witness $d$, and let
$i$ be a subject with $z_i = 0$. If $g(t; c_i) \neq 0$ for some
$t \in \{T_i\} \cup \{\text{quadrature nodes for } i\}$, then $v_i$ is
uniquely determined by $d$, namely $v_i = -x_i(t)^{\top}d / g(t; c_i)$.

*Proof.* Immediate from requirement (T) at that $t$. $\square$

Since $d$ is already pinned by the subjects whose data does determine the
ratio, and since under (S) those subjects all agree on a single structural
value, Proposition 5 says that a silent subject's entry is not free at all
in the joint model: it must take that same consensus value. This gives a
stronger justification for the implementation's behavior than the one
recorded in the source. The `BUG FIX` comment in `_absorbable_basis`
motivates imputing the median of the determined ratios on the grounds that
the alternative left $Q[:,0]$ non-uniform and so projected out a
subject-weighted quantity rather than the simple mean. Proposition 5 shows
the imputation is not merely tidier: the previous fallback of $s_i = 0$
produced a direction that is *not* in $\mathcal{A}$, so the old code swept
a direction the survival submodel does identify, while the median
imputation is the unique choice consistent with joint-model invariance.
The empirical symptom recorded in `dev/diag_slope_projection.R` -
$\overline{b_{i1}}$ left at 0.04-0.07 instead of pinned near machine zero -
is the visible trace of that. (Checked against the shipped code: with five
baseline-only subjects among twenty-five, the returned basis vector is
uniform to $2.7 \times 10^{-17}$.)

### 4.7 What this does and does not establish

**Corollary 1 (model invariance).** Let $v \in \mathcal{A}$ with witness
$d$. Then for any parameter values, replacing $(\beta, b)$ by
$(\beta + c\,d,\; b + c\,v\,e_{q_\ast}^{\top})$ leaves $\mu_{ij}$,
$m_i(t)$, the hazard, and hence the entire joint likelihood exactly
unchanged. Consequently the set of achievable mean structures is identical
with and without the reparameterization.

This is the claim Section 3.4 makes informally and Section 5 verifies
empirically, and Propositions 2, 3 and 5 establish it for the directions
the implementation actually removes, given (S).

It is worth being exact about the boundary of the result. What is proved
is *likelihood* invariance. What is not proved, and does not follow, is
anything about the posterior. The reparameterized column
$b[\,\cdot\,, q_\ast]$ is supported on the orthogonal complement of
$\operatorname{span}(Q)$, a proper subspace, so the implied prior is
singular there, while `sigma_b` continues to govern the unconstrained
`b_raw` and the swept directions sample their prior unmodified. A
construction can be provably likelihood-invariant and still be
miscalibrated; indeed `wishart_gibbs_centered` was likelihood-invariant in
the same sense and was found wanting on precisely that axis.

An earlier version of this document left that as an open question and
offered a conjecture: that because this construction changes the prior's
*support* rather than imposing an exact Gibbs constraint, it might escape
the failure mode. **That conjecture is false, and the simulation in
Section 9.1 refutes it.** The credible intervals for exactly the swept
parameters are too narrow by close to the predicted
$\sigma_b/\sqrt{N}$ - measured $\mathrm{sd\_ratio} = 0.283$ against
$1.177$ for an unmodified fit, with 95% coverage $0.50$ against $1.00$ -
while point estimates remain unbiased and the negative control is
untouched. The mechanism is not subtle in hindsight: the swept component
of `b_raw` is, after the sweep, unconstrained by the likelihood, so it
samples its prior, and nothing carries that uncertainty into $\beta$'s
posterior.

This is a statement about the *coordinates in which the sampler reports*,
not about the sampler's target being wrong, and that distinction turns out
to be actionable. Section 4.9 shows that the discarded uncertainty can be
restored exactly, in closed form, from the draws the same fit already
produces.

### 4.8 What the implementation now does

Three concrete items followed from the analysis above, in descending order
of importance. All three have since been implemented; this subsection
records what ships rather than what was recommended.

1. **The completeness failure is closed, not merely detected.** The
   column-wise search has been superseded by the null-space computation of
   Section 4.5, implemented as `_absorbable_basis_exact()`: one SVD of a
   $\left(\sum_i n_i\right) \times p$ matrix, basis-independent, and
   provably exact by Proposition 4. It is now *authoritative* - the basis
   actually swept. The column-wise `_absorbable_basis()` is retained
   alongside it for **attribution**, because it names *which* columns of
   $X$ expose each direction, which is what makes the fit's report
   diagnostic rather than a bare dimension count. The two are compared at
   every fit and any disagreement raises a warning naming the extra
   directions; the reverse disagreement (the exact construction finding
   *fewer*) would contradict Proposition 2 and is reported as a bug.
   `fit$convergence$orthogonalize` carries `n_directions_column_search`
   separately, so the spline/polynomial case is detectable
   programmatically rather than by parsing warning text. Every returned
   direction is verified against the defining identity before use, so the
   basis is sound by construction rather than by choice of tolerance.
2. **Condition (S) is checked, not assumed.**
   `_structural_extension_residual()` evaluates the same proportionality
   on `X_time_surv`/`Z_time_surv` and `X_time_quad`/`Z_time_quad` - arrays
   the backend already builds - and warns when the worst relative residual
   exceeds $10^{-6}$, stating explicitly that results from such a fit are
   unvalidated. (S) has thus moved from an argument in this document to a
   per-fit assertion.
3. **Proposition 5's justification is recorded at the site.** The source
   comment previously presented the median fallback as restoring
   uniformity, which is the visible symptom rather than the reason; it now
   states that the silent subject's entry is *forced* by joint-model
   invariance, since the survival submodel identifies what the
   longitudinal submodel alone does not.

None of the three changes any number reported in Sections 5 through 7:
every design used in this document spells `time` as its own column, so
$K$ contains it, (C) holds, and both constructions agree exactly there.
`dev/verify_absorbable_basis.py` checks that agreement directly, across
the canonical designs and a randomized sweep, so the claim is a test
rather than an assurance.

### 4.9 Restoring the identified parameterization: an exact correction

Section 4.7 establishes that the reparameterization is likelihood-
invariant but not posterior-preserving, and Section 9.1 measures the
consequence. This subsection shows the consequence is *removable*: the
discarded uncertainty can be restored exactly, in closed form, from the
draws an orthogonalized fit already produces. No second fit is required,
and no sampled quantity changes.

The idea is that the sweep does not destroy information, it only moves
it. The component $Q^{\top} b_{\mathrm{raw}}[\,\cdot\,, q_\ast]$ removed
from $b$ is still present in the draws - `b_raw` is a deterministic
function of the sampled `b_std`, `sigma_b` and `L_corr` - and by
Definition 1 its effect on the fitted values is *exactly* reproducible by
a shift in $\beta$. Recovering the unconstrained parameterization is
therefore a matter of applying that shift.

**Prior work.** The same construction appears, for a spatial random
effect in a linear or generalized linear model, in the restricted spatial
regression literature (Reich, Hodges & Zadnik 2006; Hughes & Haran 2013,
who also motivate the restriction computationally). Hanks et al. (2015,
eq. 17) give the bijection $\delta = \beta + (X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}\eta$
between the unrestricted model's coefficients $\beta$ and the restricted
model's $\delta$, under which the two likelihoods coincide, and Bradley
(2024) states the corresponding posterior equivalence in general form.
Definition 2 and Propositions 6-7 below are the joint-model analogue of the
inverse map - restricted to unrestricted, hence the opposite sign - with
the absorbable set $\mathcal{A}$ in place of the column space of $X$ and
Condition (S) carrying the argument through the survival submodel. The
narrow intervals of the uncorrected, restricted coefficient that Section
9.1 measures are likewise the joint-model counterpart of Khan & Calder's
(2022) finding for restricted spatial regression. Earlier versions of
this section did not cite this literature.

**Definition 2 (generator map).** Let $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}$ be
the orthonormal basis of swept directions, with
$\operatorname{span}(Q) \subseteq \mathcal{A}$ by Proposition 3. For each
column $Q[\,\cdot\,, m]$ Proposition 1 supplies a witness $d$; write it as
$-\Gamma e_m$, so that

$$X_i\,(\Gamma e_m) \;=\; Q[\,\cdot\,, m]_i\, z_i \quad \text{for every } i,
\qquad
x_i(t)^{\top}(\Gamma e_m) \;=\; Q[\,\cdot\,, m]_i\, g(t; c_i)
\quad \text{for every } t, \tag{G}$$

the second identity holding under (S). Extending linearly gives
$\Gamma: \mathbb{R}^{k} \to \mathbb{R}^{p}$ with
$X_i(\Gamma c) = (Qc)_i z_i$ and
$x_i(t)^{\top}(\Gamma c) = (Qc)_i\, g(t; c_i)$ for every $c \in
\mathbb{R}^{k}$.

(The sign is a convention: Definition 1 pairs a shift $+v$ in $b$ with a
witness $d$ satisfying $X_i d = -v_i z_i$, whereas $\Gamma$ is defined so
that $X_i \Gamma c = +(Qc)_i z_i$, which is the form the implementation
uses. The two differ by a sign only.)

$\Gamma$ need not be unique: if $\ker\mathcal{T} \neq \{0\}$ - that is, if
some $d \neq 0$ has $X_i d = 0$ for every $i$ - then $\Gamma$ may be
modified by any map into $\ker\mathcal{T}$. This is harmless, because
$\ker\mathcal{T}$ is exactly the set of directions along which the
likelihood is flat in $\beta$, so two choices of $\Gamma$ produce
corrected draws differing only within a subspace in which $\beta$ is
itself unidentified. When $X$ has full column rank across subjects - the
generic case, and one already required for $\beta$ to be estimable -
$\ker\mathcal{T} = \{0\}$ and $\Gamma$ is unique.

**Proposition 6 (the correction is an exact reparameterization).** Fix
$\Gamma$ satisfying (G) and define

$$\Phi:\; (\beta,\, b_{\mathrm{raw}}) \;\longmapsto\;
(\tilde\beta,\, b_{\mathrm{raw}}),
\qquad
\tilde\beta \;=\; \beta \;-\; \Gamma\big(Q^{\top}
b_{\mathrm{raw}}[\,\cdot\,, q_\ast]\big).$$

Then, writing $b^{\mathrm{orth}}$ for the swept random effects
$b_{\mathrm{raw}} - QQ^{\top}b_{\mathrm{raw}}$ on column $q_\ast$:

(i) $\Phi$ is an affine bijection with unit Jacobian determinant;

(ii) the orthogonalized model's linear predictors at
$(\beta, b_{\mathrm{raw}})$ coincide with the *unconstrained* model's at
$\Phi(\beta, b_{\mathrm{raw}})$, for every observation and every $t$:

$$\mu_{ij}\big(\beta,\, b^{\mathrm{orth}}\big)
= \mu_{ij}\big(\tilde\beta,\, b_{\mathrm{raw}}\big),
\qquad
m_i\big(t;\, \beta,\, b^{\mathrm{orth}}\big)
= m_i\big(t;\, \tilde\beta,\, b_{\mathrm{raw}}\big);$$

(iii) consequently the two likelihoods agree exactly,
$L^{\mathrm{orth}}(\beta, b_{\mathrm{raw}}, \theta) =
L(\tilde\beta, b_{\mathrm{raw}}, \theta)$ for all remaining parameters
$\theta$.

*Proof.* Write $c = Q^{\top} b_{\mathrm{raw}}[\,\cdot\,, q_\ast]$, so the
removed component is $QQ^{\top}b_{\mathrm{raw}}[\,\cdot\,, q_\ast] = Qc$.
Only column $q_\ast$ is altered, so

$$\mu_{ij}\big(\beta, b^{\mathrm{orth}}\big)
= x_{ij}^{\top}\beta + z_{ij}^{\top}b_i - (Qc)_i\, z_{ij,q_\ast}.$$

By the first identity in (G), $(Qc)_i z_i = X_i(\Gamma c)$, which read
componentwise is $(Qc)_i z_{ij,q_\ast} = x_{ij}^{\top}\Gamma c$.
Substituting,

$$\mu_{ij}\big(\beta, b^{\mathrm{orth}}\big)
= x_{ij}^{\top}\big(\beta - \Gamma c\big) + z_{ij}^{\top}b_i
= x_{ij}^{\top}\tilde\beta + z_{ij}^{\top}b_i
= \mu_{ij}\big(\tilde\beta, b_{\mathrm{raw}}\big).$$

The same computation with the second identity in (G) gives the trajectory
statement for every $t \in [0,\tau]$; this is the step that requires (S),
and it is the only place the survival submodel enters. Since the joint
likelihood depends on $(\beta, b)$ only through $\mu$ and $m$, (iii)
follows. For (i), $\Phi$ is the identity in $b_{\mathrm{raw}}$ and a
$b_{\mathrm{raw}}$-dependent translation in $\beta$, hence block-triangular
with identity diagonal blocks. $\square$

When several columns are swept at once (`orthogonalize_b`), the shifts add:
$\tilde\beta = \beta - \sum_{q} \Gamma_q\big(Q_q^{\top}
b_{\mathrm{raw}}[\,\cdot\,, q]\big)$, each term justified by Proposition 6
applied to its own column.

Proposition 6 is a statement about the likelihood. The question that
matters for reporting is what happens to the *posterior*, and the answer
is exact enough to be worth stating as an identity rather than an
approximation.

**Proposition 7 (posterior push-forward).** Suppose the orthogonalized and
unconstrained models are given the same priors $\pi(\beta)$,
$\pi(b_{\mathrm{std}})$, $\pi(\theta)$ - as they are, since the
reparameterization alters only how $b$ enters the likelihood, never any
prior. Let $p^{\mathrm{orth}}$ and $p$ denote the two posteriors. Then

$$\big(\Phi_{\#}\, p^{\mathrm{orth}}\big)
\big(\tilde\beta,\, b_{\mathrm{raw}},\, \theta \mid y\big)
\;\propto\;
\underbrace{\frac{\pi\big(\tilde\beta + s\big)}{\pi\big(\tilde\beta\big)}}
_{\textstyle w(\tilde\beta,\, b_{\mathrm{raw}})}
\;\cdot\;
p\big(\tilde\beta,\, b_{\mathrm{raw}},\, \theta \mid y\big),
\qquad
s \;=\; \Gamma\big(Q^{\top}b_{\mathrm{raw}}[\,\cdot\,, q_\ast]\big).$$

In particular:

(i) if $\pi(\beta)$ is invariant under translation by
$\operatorname{range}\Gamma$ - a flat prior on that subspace, for instance
- then $w \equiv 1$ and the corrected draws are *exact* draws from the
unconstrained model's posterior;

(ii) for $\pi(\beta) = \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\beta^{2} I_p)$, which is what
`jmjax` uses,

$$\log w
= -\,\frac{2\,\tilde\beta^{\top} s + \lVert s \rVert^{2}}
{2\,\sigma_\beta^{2}}.$$

*Proof.* The orthogonalized posterior is
$p^{\mathrm{orth}} \propto \pi(\beta)\,\pi(b_{\mathrm{raw}} \mid \theta)\,
\pi(\theta)\, L^{\mathrm{orth}}(\beta, b_{\mathrm{raw}}, \theta)$. For
fixed $(b_{\mathrm{raw}}, \theta)$ the quantity $s$ is constant and
$\beta \mapsto \tilde\beta = \beta - s$ is a translation with unit
Jacobian, so the density of $\tilde\beta$ is obtained by substituting
$\beta = \tilde\beta + s$:

$$\Phi_{\#}\,p^{\mathrm{orth}}
\;\propto\;
\pi\big(\tilde\beta + s\big)\,\pi(b_{\mathrm{raw}} \mid \theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,
L^{\mathrm{orth}}\big(\tilde\beta + s,\, b_{\mathrm{raw}},\, \theta\big).$$

By Proposition 6(iii), $L^{\mathrm{orth}}(\tilde\beta + s, b_{\mathrm{raw}},
\theta) = L(\tilde\beta, b_{\mathrm{raw}}, \theta)$. Comparing with
$p \propto \pi(\tilde\beta)\,\pi(b_{\mathrm{raw}} \mid \theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,
L(\tilde\beta, b_{\mathrm{raw}}, \theta)$ gives the stated ratio; (i) and
(ii) are immediate. $\square$

Two consequences are worth drawing out, because together they explain both
why the correction works and where it would stop working.

**Corollary 2 (scale of the restored variance, and of the residual
weight).** In the canonical case $q_\ast = 0$ with $z_i = \mathbf{1}$ and
$Q = \mathbf{1}/\sqrt{N}$, the generator is
$\Gamma e_1 = e_{\mathrm{int}}/\sqrt{N}$ and the shift is
$s = \bar b_0\, e_{\mathrm{int}}$ - precisely the mean random intercept.
Since $\bar b_0 = O_p\big(\sigma_{b_0}/\sqrt{N}\big)$, the correction
restores exactly the $\sigma_b/\sqrt{N}$ of location uncertainty that
Section 3.2 identifies as the width of the degeneracy and that Section 9.1
measures as missing. The residual prior weight is then
$\log w = O_p\big(\lVert\beta\rVert\,\sigma_b / (\sigma_\beta^{2}
\sqrt{N})\big)$, which is negligible whenever the prior on $\beta$ is
diffuse relative to $\sigma_b/\sqrt{N}$: at $\sigma_\beta = 5$,
$\sigma_{b_0} = 0.8$ and $N = 300$, $\lVert s \rVert \approx 0.046$ and
the log-weight varies across draws by order $10^{-2}$.

So the corrected draws are not merely approximately right; they are exact
draws from the unconstrained posterior up to a reweighting whose magnitude
is known in closed form and is, under any diffuse prior on $\beta$,
numerically irrelevant. This is a sharper statement than a coverage study
can produce, and it also supplies a per-fit diagnostic rather than a
general assurance: $w$ is computable draw by draw from quantities already
stored, so the effective sample size of $\{w\}$ measures directly whether
the reweighting matters for a given fit. Implementing that diagnostic is
listed in Section 9.3.

**Where the correction fails.** Three conditions, each already visible in
the statements above:

1. **Condition (S) must hold.** Proposition 6(ii) uses the second identity
   in (G) for all $t$, so a design that fails (S) breaks the correction
   for exactly the same reason it breaks the sweep. The existing (S) check
   therefore guards both. Verified directly for the design of Example 1:
   the residual is $3 \times 10^{-16}$ on the survival and quadrature
   grids, so the correction is valid precisely where the completeness
   repair is most needed.
2. **The prior on $\beta$ must be diffuse relative to
   $\sigma_b/\sqrt{N}$.** Otherwise $w$ departs from 1 and the corrected
   draws require the weight to be applied, not merely noted. Corollary 2
   bounds when this arises; a genuinely informative prior on a swept
   coefficient is the case to watch.
3. **$\Gamma$ must be computable from the same generators as $Q$.** The
   implementation obtains it by applying to the witnesses the same linear
   combination that QR applies to the directions, and verifies the
   resulting identity before use; `dev/verify_beta_correction.py` checks
   this independently of any MCMC run.

### 4.10 Why the corrected estimand mixed slowly, and an exact rotation that fixes it

Section 9.1.1 measures that `beta_corrected` inherits almost none of the
swept coefficient's efficiency gain, and Section 9.1.2 measures that
rotating `b_std[:, 0]` recovers most of it. This subsection explains both
measurements, states when the recovery is guaranteed and when it is not,
and derives two changes to the construction that the theory predicts will
carry it to the slope column and to strongly correlated random effects.
The results come in three grades, kept separate on purpose. Lemma 1 and
Propositions 8 and 9 are exact for the full joint model. Proposition 10 is
exact for the model with the variance components held fixed, under the
oracle diagonal metric that NUTS's adaptation estimates; with the variance
components sampled, it describes the conditional geometry that sampling
averages over. The step from
that geometry to effective sample size is a stylised model of NUTS, and is
labelled as one.

**Setting.** The random effects are sampled non-centred:
$b_{\mathrm{raw}} = b_{\mathrm{std}} L^{\top}$, with the entries of
$b_{\mathrm{std}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times q}$ independent
$\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ a priori and $L = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_b)\,
L_{\mathrm{corr}}$ lower-triangular. For $q = 2$,

$$L = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_0 & 0 \\ \rho\,\sigma_1 & s\,\sigma_1
\end{pmatrix}, \qquad s = \sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}.$$

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the set of swept columns ($\{0\}$ for
`orthogonalize_b0`; every column with a non-empty basis for
`orthogonalize_b`), $Q_j \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k_j}$ the orthonormal
basis swept from column $j$, and $Q_{\cup} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}$ an
orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{span}\bigcup_{j \in \mathcal{S}} Q_j$.
The swept random effects are $b = \operatorname{sw}(b_{\mathrm{raw}})$,
where $\operatorname{sw}(W)[\,\cdot\,, j] = (I - Q_j Q_j^{\top})\,
W[\,\cdot\,, j]$ for $j \in \mathcal{S}$ and $W[\,\cdot\,, j]$ otherwise,
and the orthogonalized likelihood $L^{\mathrm{orth}}$ depends on
$b_{\mathrm{std}}$ only through $b$. Write $\theta$ for every other
parameter, including $\beta$, $\sigma_b$ and $L_{\mathrm{corr}}$.

**Definition 3 (flat subspace).** For fixed $\theta$,
$\mathcal{F}(\theta) = \{\Delta \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times q} :
\operatorname{sw}(\Delta L^{\top}) = 0\}$.

Because $\operatorname{sw}$ is linear, $L^{\mathrm{orth}}$ is unchanged by
$b_{\mathrm{std}} \mapsto b_{\mathrm{std}} + \Delta$ for every
$\Delta \in \mathcal{F}(\theta)$. These are exactly the directions that,
in Section 9.1's words, "simply sample their prior".

**Lemma 1 (where the flat subspace lives).** $\Delta \in
\mathcal{F}(\theta)$ if and only if $\Delta = W (L^{\top})^{-1}$ for some
$W$ with $W[\,\cdot\,, j] \in \operatorname{span}(Q_j)$ for
$j \in \mathcal{S}$ and $W[\,\cdot\,, j] = 0$ otherwise. Hence
$\dim \mathcal{F}(\theta) = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} k_j$, and every
column of every $\Delta \in \mathcal{F}(\theta)$ lies in
$\operatorname{span}(Q_{\cup})$ - for every value of $\theta$, even though
$\mathcal{F}(\theta)$ itself moves with $L$.

*Proof.* Put $W = \Delta L^{\top}$; $L$ is invertible. $\operatorname{sw}
(W) = 0$ holds exactly when every swept column satisfies
$(I - Q_j Q_j^{\top}) W[\,\cdot\,, j] = 0$, that is
$W[\,\cdot\,, j] \in \operatorname{span}(Q_j)$, and every unswept column is
zero. $W \mapsto W (L^{\top})^{-1}$ is a bijection, which gives the
dimension, and each column of $W (L^{\top})^{-1}$ is a linear combination
of columns of $W$, all of which lie in $\operatorname{span}(Q_{\cup})$.
$\square$

For the case every pilot in this document used ($q = 2$,
$\mathcal{S} = \{0\}$, $Q_{\cup} = Q_0$), Lemma 1 gives the flat subspace
explicitly. With $W = [\,Q_0 c,\; 0\,]$ and
$(L^{\top})^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sigma_0 & -\rho/(s\sigma_0) \\
0 & 1/(s\sigma_1) \end{pmatrix}$,

$$\Delta = \frac{1}{s\,\sigma_0}\,\big[\; s\,Q_0 c,\;\; -\rho\,Q_0 c
\;\big]:$$

each flat direction is $s$ parts intercept column and $-\rho$ parts slope
column, both along $\operatorname{span}(Q_0)$. Only at $\rho = 0$ does it
lie entirely in the intercept column.

**Proposition 8 (fixed rotations are exact).** Let
$R = [\,Q_{\cup} \mid Q_{\perp}\,]$ be any fixed $N \times N$ orthogonal
matrix, and $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \{0, \dots, q-1\}$ any set of columns.
Reparameterize $b_{\mathrm{std}}[\,\cdot\,, j] = Q_{\cup} U[\,\cdot\,, j]
+ Q_{\perp} V[\,\cdot\,, j]$ for $j \in \mathcal{C}$ (other columns
unchanged), with independent $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ priors on the entries of
$U \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times \lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert}$ and
$V \in \mathbb{R}^{(N-k) \times \lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert}$.
Then (i) the map $(U, V) \mapsto b_{\mathrm{std}}$ is linear with
$\lvert\det\rvert = 1$; (ii) the prior it induces on $b_{\mathrm{std}}$ is
exactly the original one; (iii) consequently the posterior of every model
quantity - $\beta$, $b_{\mathrm{raw}}$, $b$, $\theta$ and `beta_corrected`
- is identical to the unrotated parameterization's, and so is every
calibration property of every estimand, up to Monte Carlo error; and (iv)
$U[\,\cdot\,, j] = Q_{\cup}^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}[\,\cdot\,, j]$.

*Proof.* On each rotated column the map is multiplication by the
orthogonal $R$, so $\lvert\det\rvert = 1$ and
$R\,\mathcal{N}(0, I_N) = \mathcal{N}(0, R R^{\top}) = \mathcal{N}(0, I_N)$,
giving (i) and (ii). The likelihood is a function of $b_{\mathrm{std}}$
and $\theta$, whose joint prior is unchanged, so the posterior pushed
forward to the original coordinates is unchanged: (iii). (iv) follows from
$Q_{\cup}^{\top} Q_{\perp} = 0$. $\square$

`orthogonalize_b0_rotate` as implemented is the case
$\mathcal{C} = \{0\}$, $Q_{\cup} = Q_0$, with $Q_{\perp}$ a seeded random
completion. Proposition 8(iii) is why Section 9.1.2's $R = 100$
calibration comparison came out as it did: equality between `D` and
`D_rot` was predicted exactly, so that study tested the *implementation* -
a bug would have shown up as a difference - rather than the construction.

**Proposition 9 (the flat coordinates are a posteriori exactly their
prior).** Fix $\theta$, let $B_{\theta}$ be an orthonormal basis of
$\mathcal{F}(\theta)$ (Frobenius inner product), and let $\xi$ and $\zeta$
be the coordinates of $b_{\mathrm{std}}$ along $\mathcal{F}(\theta)$ and
along its orthogonal complement. Then, under the full joint model,

$$p(\xi \mid \zeta, \theta, y) \;=\; \mathcal{N}\big(\xi;\, 0,\,
I_{\dim\mathcal{F}}\big).$$

Because the right-hand side does not involve $(\zeta, \theta)$, $\xi$ is a
posteriori exactly standard normal and independent of $(\zeta, \theta)$,
even though the subspace it is measured along moves with $\theta$.

*Proof.* The prior on $b_{\mathrm{std}}$ is rotation-invariant, so
$(\xi, \zeta) \mid \theta$ are independent standard normal.
$L^{\mathrm{orth}}$ depends on $b_{\mathrm{std}}$ only through
$\operatorname{sw}(b_{\mathrm{std}} L^{\top})$, which by construction
depends on $\zeta$ alone. Hence
$p(\xi, \zeta, \theta \mid y) \propto \pi(\theta)\,
\mathcal{N}(\xi; 0, I)\, \mathcal{N}(\zeta; 0, I)\,
L^{\mathrm{orth}}(\zeta, \theta)$, which factorizes in $\xi$. (Only the
fact that the likelihood sees the swept $b$ is used; Condition (S) is
what gives `beta_corrected` its meaning, not what makes $\xi$ flat.)
$\square$

This is the standard fact that data carry no information about
non-identified parameters beyond what the identified ones carry (Dawid
1979; Poirier 1998; Gustafson 2015). What Proposition 9 adds is the
location of those parameters in `jmjax`'s own coordinates, and the
observation that they carry most of `beta_corrected`'s uncertainty: by
Proposition 6, `beta_corrected` $= \tilde\beta = \beta - \Gamma\,\sigma_0\,
Q_0^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}[\,\cdot\,, 0]$ with $\beta$ the sampled, swept
coefficient, and in the closed-form check below the flat coordinates carry
87-96% of its posterior variance at $\lvert\rho\rvert \le 0.3$, falling to
about 27% at $\rho = 0.9$.

**Corollary 3 (the intercept-only case).** Take $q = 2$,
$\mathcal{S} = \{0\}$, and write $u = Q_0^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}
[\,\cdot\,, 0]$ and $w = Q_0^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}[\,\cdot\,, 1]$ for the
intercept and slope columns' generator coordinates. The flat coordinates
are $\xi = s\,u - \rho\,w$, and the identified coordinates in the same
plane are $\eta = \rho\,u + s\,w$; equivalently $u = s\,\xi + \rho\,\eta$
and $w = -\rho\,\xi + s\,\eta$. Consequently:

(i) if $\rho = 0$, $u$ is a posteriori exactly $\mathcal{N}(0, I_k)$ and
independent of everything else, so the covariance a dense mass block on
$u$ would try to learn is the identity. $\rho = 0$ has probability zero
under a sampled correlation, and the pilots generated data at
$\rho = 0.3$; but Proposition 10(b) below shows that once $u$ is its own
coordinate, what remains slow lies along $w$, in the slope column, which a
dense block on $u$ alone cannot reach. Either way, the pilots' finding
that `dense_mass_b0_generator` adds nothing (Section 9.1.2) is what the
theory predicts;

(ii) if $\rho \neq 0$, a fraction $\rho^{2}$ of each flat direction lies
along $w$ - outside the rotated block, spread across the slope column's
per-subject coordinates. The current rotation therefore captures the flat
subspace completely only at $\rho = 0$.

*Proof.* Normalize the direction given after Lemma 1. $\square$

**Proposition 10 (what a diagonal metric sees, with the variance
components fixed).** Hold the variance components
$\psi = (\sigma_b, \rho, \sigma_e)$ fixed. Let $\Sigma$ be the posterior
covariance of the sampled coordinates and $M = \operatorname{diag}(\Sigma)$
the oracle diagonal metric - the inverse mass matrix (NumPyro's
`inverse_mass_matrix`) that windowed adaptation estimates. For a direction
$\delta$ write $\mathcal{R}(\delta) = \delta^{\top}\Sigma\,\delta \big/
\delta^{\top} M \delta$ for its variance after whitening by $M$; by
Courant-Fischer $M^{-1/2}\Sigma M^{-1/2}$ has an eigenvalue at least
$\mathcal{R}(\delta)$, so a large $\mathcal{R}$ certifies a slow direction.
Take $q = 2$, $\mathcal{S} = \{0\}$, a column $g = Q_0[\,\cdot\,, m]$, the
generator coordinates $u_m = g^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}[\,\cdot\,, 0]$ and
$w_m = g^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}[\,\cdot\,, 1]$ of Corollary 3, the
posterior variance $\lambda_m \ge 0$ of the identified combination
$\eta_m = \rho u_m + s w_m$, and the marginal posterior variances $m_{j,i}$
of $b_{\mathrm{std}}[i, j]$, with $\bar m_j = \sum_i g_i^{2} m_{j,i}$.
Then

$$\operatorname{Var}(u_m) = s^{2} + \rho^{2}\lambda_m, \quad
\operatorname{Var}(w_m) = \rho^{2} + s^{2}\lambda_m, \quad
\operatorname{Cov}(u_m, w_m) = -\rho s\,(1 - \lambda_m),$$

and:

(a) *plain `orthogonalize_b0`*: $\mathcal{R}(u_m) = (s^{2} +
\rho^{2}\lambda_m)/\bar m_0$, $\mathcal{R}(w_m) = (\rho^{2} +
s^{2}\lambda_m)/\bar m_1$, and for the flat direction itself
$\mathcal{R}(\xi_m) = 1/(s^{2}\bar m_0 + \rho^{2}\bar m_1)$;

(b) *column 0 rotated, as implemented*: $\mathcal{R}(u_m) = 1$ and
$\mathcal{R}(\xi_m) \le 1/s^{4}$, but $\mathcal{R}(w_m)$ is exactly as in
(a);

(c) *every column rotated by $Q_0$*: $u_m$ and $w_m$ are both coordinates,
and the whitened covariance restricted to them is their correlation
matrix, so every direction in their plane has
$\mathcal{R} \in [1 - \lvert r_m\rvert,\, 1 + \lvert r_m\rvert] \subseteq
[0, 2]$, where
$r_m = -\rho s (1 - \lambda_m) \big/ \sqrt{(s^{2} + \rho^{2}\lambda_m)
(\rho^{2} + s^{2}\lambda_m)}$. With $q$ random-effect columns the same
argument gives $[0, q]$.

*Proof.* By Proposition 9 with $\psi$ fixed, $\xi_m = s u_m - \rho w_m$ has
unit variance and is uncorrelated with $\eta_m$; inverting,
$u_m = s\xi_m + \rho\eta_m$ and $w_m = -\rho\xi_m + s\eta_m$, which gives
the three moments. In the unrotated coordinates $u_m$ is the direction
$(g, 0)$ and $w_m$ the direction $(0, g)$, so their denominators are
$\bar m_0$ and $\bar m_1$; the flat direction is $(s g, -\rho g)$, giving
(a). In (b), $u_m$ is a coordinate, whose diagonal metric entry is its own
variance, so $\mathcal{R}(u_m) = 1$; for the flat direction
$\delta^{\top} M \delta = s^{2}\operatorname{Var}(u_m) + \rho^{2}\bar m_1
\ge s^{4}$; and column 1 is untouched, so $\mathcal{R}(w_m)$ is unchanged.
In (c) the restriction of $M^{-1/2}\Sigma M^{-1/2}$ to the two coordinates
is their correlation matrix, whose eigenvalues are $1 \pm \lvert r_m\rvert$,
and every Rayleigh quotient lies between them; a $q \times q$ correlation
matrix has eigenvalues in $[0, q]$. $\square$

*Reading Proposition 10.* The $m_{j,i}$ are per-subject shrinkage factors,
small when each subject's own data pin down its own random effects: many
visits, small $\sigma_e$ relative to $\sigma_b$. (In a random-intercept-
only Gaussian model $m_{0,i} = (1 + n_i\sigma_0^{2}/\sigma_e^{2})^{-1}$
exactly; a random slope enlarges them through within-subject
intercept-slope confounding, but the dependence runs the same way.) They
are $g$-weighted averages, so they do not shrink with $N$. Part (a) says
both generator coordinates are slow under the plain sweep: at the pilots'
design `dev/theory_rotation_toy.py` gives $\mathcal{R}(u_m) \approx 14$,
rising to 22-31 with 8-20 visits per subject. Part (b) says that under the
current rotation $u$ is no longer certified slow (every coordinate has
$\mathcal{R} = 1$ under an oracle diagonal metric), but $w$ still is, and
its variance contains a $\rho^{2}$ share of the flat direction.
`beta_corrected` for the intercept depends on $u$ alone, but $u$ and $w$
are correlated ($\lvert r_m\rvert$ from 0.59 to 0.99 in the toy at
$\sigma_e = 0.3$ with 2-11 or 8-20 visits and $\rho \ge 0.3$; 0.29-0.46
with 2-4 visits), so a slow $w$ drags $u$ with it. The drag needs both a
large $\mathcal{R}(w)$, which falls as $\lvert\rho\rvert$ grows, and a
large $\lvert r_m\rvert$, which rises with it, so it peaks at intermediate
$\rho$ and grows with the information about individual slopes. Part (c)
says that rotating every column makes each generator row's plane
coordinate-aligned: within a row no direction is slower than $q$ times the
scale of its own coordinates, whatever the data, $N$ or $\rho$. Across
rows the coordinates can still be correlated through the identified
combinations $\eta$, so the only general bound for the whole
$k \times q$ block is $kq$; in the toy the whole block stays below 2 in
all 24 designs, for both `D` and `E`. What (c)
does not bound is the fast side: when $\lvert r_m\rvert$ is near 1 the
plane also contains a narrow direction ($1 - \lvert r_m\rvert$), which can
shrink NUTS's step size. A dense mass block on the $k \times q$ generator
block, or the $\theta$-dependent rotation of Corollary 4, removes it.

**From geometry to effective sample size (a model, not a theorem).** HMC's
step size is limited by the narrowest whitened direction, and NUTS's
trajectory length is set largely by the bulk of the whitened spectrum
(Neal 2011, Sections 4.1-4.4; Hoffman & Gelman 2014) - the second half
of that sentence is the modelling assumption. A direction whose
whitened variance $\Lambda$ exceeds the bulk's is then crossed
diffusively, with an integrated autocorrelation time (IAT) growing roughly
linearly in $\Lambda$. That diagonal preconditioning need not remove a
poorly scaled direction oblique to the coordinate axes - and can even make
conditioning worse - is shown by example in Hird & Livingstone (2025); the regression-level instance of the same problem is what Stan's
QR reparameterization addresses (Stan Development Team, *User's Guide*,
"The QR reparameterization"). What is specific here is where the direction
is (Lemma 1), that its whitened variance grows with per-subject
information (Proposition 10(a)), and that a fixed rotation aligns it with
the axes without changing the model (Proposition 8). In a stylised model -
exact Hamiltonian dynamics, integration time uniform on $[0, 2T_0]$ with
$T_0$ set by the bulk - a direction of whitened variance $\Lambda$ has
IAT $(1 + r)/(1 - r)$ with $r = \sin(\pi/\sqrt{\Lambda})\big/
(\pi/\sqrt{\Lambda})$, $\Lambda$ measured relative to the bulk (the
median whitened eigenvalue, 0.97-1.17 in the toy): 1 at $\Lambda = 1$,
about $1.2\,\Lambda$ for large $\Lambda$.

This also revises Section 9.1.1's diagnosis. There, the slow mixing was
attributed to the `b` block's own funnel-type conditioning under
`sigma_b`. The closed-form check below holds every variance component
fixed - so no funnel can arise - and still produces slow mixing of the
corrected estimands under the plain sweep (IAT 13-34 iterations for the
intercept) and its repair by rotation (IAT 1-5 with the current rotation, 1-2
rotating every column). Misalignment of the
generator directions with the coordinate axes is therefore sufficient; the
funnel is not needed to explain the pattern, though with sampled variance
components it may still contribute.

**A closed-form check.** `dev/theory_rotation_toy.py` (NumPy only; 10-20
s) computes the exact posterior of the longitudinal submodel with the
variance components fixed at `dev/sim_joint.R`'s generating values and
$N = 300$. It verifies Proposition 9 (the flat coordinates' covariance
equals $I$, and their covariance with every other coordinate is zero, to
below $5 \times 10^{-13}$, for $\rho \in \{0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9\}$), and
matches every closed form in Proposition 10 - the three moments,
$\mathcal{R}$ of $u$, $w$ and $\xi$ in (a) and (b), and the plane's
eigenvalues in (c) - to within $2 \times 10^{-12}$ across 24 designs. Under the stylised NUTS model it gives these
IATs, in iterations (1 means effectively independent draws; `rot0` is the
current column-0 rotation, `rot-all` rotates every column by $Q_0$):

| visits per subject | $\rho$ | intercept: `D` | `D` + rot0 | `E` + rot0 | `E` + rot-all | slope: `E` | `E` + rot0 | `E` + rot-all |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2-11 | 0.0 | 13.0 | 1.1 | 1.1 | 1.2 | 34.9 | 43.3 | 1.9 |
| 2-11 | 0.3 | 13.9 | 1.8 | 1.8 | 1.4 | 17.1 | 20.8 | 1.6 |
| 2-11 | 0.6 | 14.8 | 2.2 | 2.3 | 1.6 | 10.9 | 7.1 | 1.3 |
| 2-11 | 0.9 | 20.3 | 1.7 | 1.5 | 1.4 | 19.8 | 1.3 | 1.1 |
| 8-20 | 0.0 | 34.0 | 1.0 | 1.1 | 1.1 | 207.2 | 160.6 | 1.0 |
| 8-20 | 0.3 | 28.5 | 3.7 | 3.8 | 1.6 | 64.3 | 66.3 | 1.1 |
| 8-20 | 0.6 | 26.4 | 4.1 | 4.5 | 1.6 | 25.4 | 17.7 | 1.1 |
| 8-20 | 0.9 | 28.1 | 2.0 | 1.8 | 1.3 | 27.1 | 1.9 | 1.1 |

Three features of this table are predictions the simulations can test.
First, the current rotation's advantage is reduced at intermediate
$\rho$ when individual slopes are well identified (8-20 visits,
$\rho = 0.3$-$0.6$, IAT 3.7-4.5 against about 1 at $\rho = 0$): Proposition
10(b)'s unrotated $w$, correlated with $u$. Rotating every column removes
the reduction. Second, the current construction leaves the slope's
corrected estimand slow except at large $\lvert\rho\rvert$, while rotating
every column repairs it at every $\rho$. Proposition 10 is stated for
`orthogonalize_b0`, so this second prediction goes slightly beyond it.
Under `orthogonalize_b` the slope's correction depends on the slope
column's generator coordinate along $Q_1$, $\rho\,u + s\,w$ in Corollary
3's notation, where both columns are swept and both combinations are
flat. The current rotation makes only $u$ a coordinate, so a share $s^{2}$
of that quantity stays along the misaligned $w$. That share is large at
small $\rho$ and small at $\rho = 0.9$, which matches the table: `E` +
rot0 slope IAT 20.8-160.6 for $\rho \le 0.3$ against 1.3-1.9 at
$\rho = 0.9$. Extending Proposition 10's statement to both columns swept
is routine along rows where both are swept, since both coordinates are
then exactly flat, but it is not written out here. Third, the
gain does not depend on $N$: for the current rotation (random completion,
as implemented) at the pilots' design, the model predicts 8.5x ESS per
gradient over `D` at $N = 150$, 300 and 600.

Against the pilots the agreement is partial, and should be read that way.
The pilots measured the rotation at 5.8x-7.6x ESS per second over arm `A`,
with `D` itself at 0.91x-1.05x of `A` - roughly 6x-8x over `D`, close to
the model's 8.5x (the rotated arm also took about 35% longer per fit,
which the model does not predict). But the model puts `D` at about 2x `A`
for the intercept, and `E` at 3x-4x `A` for both the intercept and the
slope, where the pilots measured about 1x and 1.3x. So the model shows
that misalignment is sufficient to make the corrected estimands mix
slowly, and it predicts the rotation's gain well; it does not reproduce
the pilots' finding that the plain sweep gains almost nothing over a
default fit. Whatever else contributes to that - sampled variance
components, the survival submodel, adaptation error - is outside it.

**Corollary 4 (two changes the theory recommends; not yet implemented).**

1. *Rotate every column by the same fixed $Q_{\cup}$* (Proposition 8 with
   $\mathcal{C}$ = all columns). By Lemma 1 this contains the flat
   subspace, for every value of $\rho$, inside an explicit $k \times q$
   block, and by Proposition 10(c) no direction within any one generator row
   is then slower, after whitening, than 2 (or $q$ with $q$ random-effect
   columns; the whole block is bounded only by $kq$ in general, though it
