   stays below 2 in the toy). This removes the obstacle `_orthogonal_complement()`'s docstring and
   Section 9.1.2 give for not extending the rotation to the slope column:
   the $\rho$-dependence is real, but it now lives inside a small, fixed
   block instead of across the per-subject coordinates. The remaining
   factor of at most 2 can be removed either by a dense mass block on
   that $k \times q$ block, or exactly, by rotating each row of $U$ by the
   $\theta$-dependent orthogonal matrix that maps it to $(\xi, \eta)$.
   That map is orthogonal in $U$ for fixed $\theta$, so its full Jacobian
   is block-triangular with unit determinant, and by Proposition 9 it
   makes $\xi$ exactly standard normal and a posteriori independent of
   everything else for every $\theta$. $\xi$ could then even be drawn
   outside NUTS altogether.
2. *Replace the seeded random completion $Q_{\perp}$ by the Householder
   completion.* Both are exact (Proposition 8) and mix identically in the
   closed-form check (within 1% at $N = 150$-600). The random completion
   is a dense $N \times (N - k)$ matrix: $O(N^{2})$ memory and
   $O(N^{2})$ work per gradient evaluation, 0.25-0.5 GB at
   $N = 8000$ depending on precision. The Householder form ($k$ reflectors) needs $O(Nk)$ for
   both, and needs no seed.

**What this establishes and what it does not.** Exact for the full joint
model: Lemma 1, Proposition 8 (including calibration invariance) and
Proposition 9. Exact conditional on the variance components: Proposition
10. Not established: that NUTS follows the stylised IAT model once the
variance components are sampled (where a genuine funnel and a
$\sigma_b$-dependent mass matrix can add difficulty), with the survival
submodel present, and with an estimated rather than oracle mass matrix;
and whether the per-iteration overhead stays small. Those are what the
simulation plan in Section 9.3 is designed to test. On that evidence, the
case for making the rotation a default rests on Proposition 8 (it cannot
change any answer) and Proposition 10(c) (after rotating every column, no
direction within a generator row is slower than $q$ times its
coordinates' own scale, whatever the data). The remaining questions are
about cost - including the narrow direction noted after Proposition 10 -
and robustness, not about correctness.

## 5. Correctness validation

Because the reparameterization cannot change the set of achievable fitted
values (Section 3.4, proved as Corollary 1 in Section 4.7), `beta`, `alpha`, and fitted values must agree between
the default fit ("arm A") and the orthogonalized fits ("arm D" =
`orthogonalize_b0` only, "arm E" = `orthogonalize_b`, full) up to Monte
Carlo error. This was checked directly in the replicated covariate-count
sweep (Section 6): comparing `alpha`'s posterior mean between arms A and D
across every `k` tested,

| k | truth | A | D |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.500 | 0.5075 | 0.5077 |
| 4 | 0.500 | 0.4854 | 0.4855 |
| 8 | 0.500 | 0.4914 | 0.4916 |
| 12 | 0.500 | 0.5164 | 0.5163 |

and `beta_1`'s posterior mean across arms A, D, and E:

| k | truth | A | D | E |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.500 | 0.4940 | 0.4940 | 0.4944 |
| 4 | 0.500 | 0.4886 | 0.4886 | 0.4882 |
| 8 | 0.500 | 0.4953 | 0.4953 | 0.4956 |
| 12 | 0.500 | 0.4991 | 0.4991 | 0.4992 |

agree to within Monte Carlo noise at every `k`, as the construction
requires. This is complemented by the study's built-in negative control,
"arm A2" - a second default-configuration fit at an independent seed, used
to build a null distribution for how much two fits of the *same* model
should differ by chance alone, so that an apparent "A vs D" difference can
be judged against genuine sampling variability rather than eyeballed.

The algebra underneath these agreements is separately machine-checked,
independently of any MCMC run, so that a future change breaking the
construction fails a test rather than quietly shifting a posterior mean.
`dev/verify_absorbable_basis.py` (34 checks) covers soundness, the
completeness repair, the consensus imputation of Section 4.6, Condition (S)
on a design built to violate it, and a randomized sweep confirming the
exact construction never loses a direction the column-wise search found.
`dev/verify_beta_correction.py` (34 checks) covers Section 4.9: that
$\Gamma$ satisfies identity (G), and that the resulting $\tilde\beta$
reproduces the unconstrained model's fitted values exactly - on
coordinate-aligned designs, on the spline/orthogonal-polynomial design of
Example 1, and with several random-effect columns swept at once. Residuals
across all cases are at machine precision ($\le 3 \times 10^{-15}$).
`tests/testthat/test-orthogonalize.R` carries the corresponding
integration tests against real fits.

## 6. Efficiency: simulated covariate-count sweep

### 6.1 Design

`dev/sim_joint.R` was generalized this session to support an arbitrary
number of extra covariates `k_extra` (previously capped at 3): baseline
covariates are `age` (re-centered at mean 0 this session, removing a
covariate-scale confound - see Section 6.1.1), `sex`, `trt`, and, beyond
those three, independent standard-normal covariates `x4, x5, ...` with
geometrically decaying true coefficients. `dev/study_orth_vs_jmbayes2.R`
runs arms `A` (default), `D` (`orthogonalize_b0`), `E` (`orthogonalize_b`),
and `J` (`JMbayes2::jm()`) across a `k` x `n` grid, resumable via a cached
CSV keyed by `(k, n, seed, arm)`.

The sweep reported here is `k in {1, 4, 8, 12}` at `n = 1000`, 3 seeds
(matching JMbayes2 across 3 independent MCMC seeds as well), with
`JMbayes2` run at 16,000 iterations / 4,000 burn-in per chain - well above
its own package default of 3,500/500 - specifically so that any
`JMbayes2` under-performance cannot be attributed to giving it fewer draws
than it needed.

#### 6.1.1 A covariate-scale confound removed before this sweep

`age` was originally simulated as `N(50, 10)` (a realistic clinical scale).
As documented separately (`vignette("jmjax-validation")`, "Covariate scale:
now handled automatically"), an uncentered covariate on that scale induces a
strong `corr(beta_0, beta_age) ~= -0.98` posterior correlation that is
*itself* expensive for NUTS, entirely independently of the random-effects
degeneracy this document is about. `jmjax`'s automatic `standardize_covariates`
already corrects for this internally, but leaving `age` uncentered in the
*simulator* would have confounded "does the random-effects degeneracy scale
with k" with "does an unrelated fixed-effects scale issue scale with k."
`age` was re-centered to `N(0, 10)` in `sim_joint.R` before this sweep was
run, isolating the effect this document is actually about.

### 6.2 Why two R-hat gates are needed

`JMbayes2`'s random-effects covariance parameters degrade sharply with `k`
(Section 6.4), which fails an all-parameters R-hat convergence gate well
before `k = 8` - but this says nothing about whether the *regression*
parameters being compared are themselves trustworthy. Mirroring the pattern
already used in the real-data study (`dev/study_realdata_aids.R`), the
sweep checks R-hat separately on (a) every sampled parameter and (b) only
`beta`, `alpha`, and `gamma` - the parameters a user would actually report.
At every `k` in this sweep, the regression-only gate **passes for every
arm, including `J`**, even where the all-parameters gate fails by several
orders of magnitude - meaning the regression-parameter comparisons below
can be trusted even in the cells where the headline "ESS/sec, all
parameters" comparison cannot.

### 6.3 Results

Regression-only figures are `min(ESS/sec)` over `{beta, alpha, gamma}` only
("the REPORTING view"); all-parameters figures are `min(ESS/sec)` over
every sampled parameter ("the CONVERGENCE view"). `beta_0` ESS is reported
separately because it is the parameter Section 3.2's degeneracy targets
directly.

| k | beta_0 ESS: A | D (x) | E (x) | E vs A, all-params ESS/sec | E vs A, regression-only ESS/sec | regression-only p-value [95% CI] |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1  | 492.7 | 5207.2 (10.6x) | 6592.5 (13.4x) | 1.12x | 14.3x | (single seed at k=1; see note) |
| 4  | 551.2 | 7503.7 (13.6x) | 6727.9 (12.2x) | 1.26x | 14.7x | (single seed at k=4; see note) |
| 8  | 624.2 | 7268.5 (11.7x) | 6514.0 (10.4x) | 1.18x (p=0.09, CI [0.94x, 1.49x]) | 13.3x | **p = 0.0064, CI [5.46x, 32.52x]** |
| 12 | 628.6 | 7121.3 (11.3x) | 7334.8 (11.7x) | 1.14x (p=0.07, CI [0.97x, 1.34x]) | 14.2x | **p = 0.0003, CI [11.79x, 17.08x]** |

*Note: p-values require >= 2 seeds; k=1 and k=4 draw on this sweep's
seed-1 (cached) plus seeds 2-3 for the point estimates shown, but the
formal significance test was run specifically at k=8 and k=12, the two
most extreme, most decisively informative cells, as the targeted
replication (see Section 6.1). The point estimates at k=1 and k=4 are
consistent with the same pattern.*

Two things stand out, both consistent with the mechanism in Section 3.3.
First, **the regression-only advantage is essentially flat across k = 1 to
12** (13.3x-14.7x point estimates; both significance tests, at the two
extremes tested, agree closely: 95% CIs of roughly [5x-33x] and [12x-17x]).
This directly falsifies the initial hypothesis that this advantage should
grow with covariate count - and is exactly what Section 3.3's mechanism
predicts, since the binding regression parameter throughout is `beta_1`,
whose degeneracy with `mean(b_i1)` does not depend on `k` at all.

Second, **the all-parameters comparison is statistically indistinguishable
from 1x at both tested points** (both 95% CIs include 1x), while the
regression-only comparison is highly significant at both. This is the
formal version of the R-hat-gate finding in 6.2: once nuisance parameters
(dominated by `rho`, which orthogonalization does not touch - see Section
8.1) are allowed to set the pace, the *aggregate* comparison is noisy and
not clearly different from parity; the real, replicated, large effect is
specific to the regression parameters the reparameterization actually
targets.

**A parameter-specific breakdown, and why it changes the reading above.**
"Regression-only" in the table above is `min(ESS/sec)` over
`{beta, alpha, gamma}`, and in every cell of this sweep the parameter
setting that minimum (`min_who_reg` in `dev/study_orth_vs_jmbayes2.R`'s own
output) is a `beta` coefficient, never `alpha`. That means the
13.3x-14.7x figure above is, in effect, a comparison of the swept `beta`
coordinate's ESS/sec between arms - exactly the coordinate Sections 9.1 and
9.1.1 show does not survive the calibration correction. Pulling `alpha`'s
own ESS/sec out of the same runs (`alpha_ess` is stored as its own column,
independently of the `min`-based composite) gives a materially different,
and materially more important, picture:

| k | A vs J (alpha) | E vs A (alpha) |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1  | 5.72x | 1.02x |
| 4  | 8.07x | 0.91x |
| 8  | 6.22x | 1.07x |
| 12 | 6.25x | 1.15x |

`jmjax`'s *default*, non-orthogonalized fit already beats `JMbayes2` on
`alpha`'s own ESS/sec by 5.7x-8.1x, flat across k, with no involvement of
`orthogonalize_b` at all - `E vs A` for `alpha` sits close to 1x throughout
(0.91x-1.15x), unlike the 11x+ effect the same ratio produces for `beta_0`
on this same sweep. Section 8 returns to what this means for how the
overall claim should be attributed.

### 6.4 JMbayes2's own degradation with k

Independently of anything about `jmjax`, `JMbayes2`'s random-effects
covariance parameter (`D.D[...]`, a fixed 2x2 block regardless of `k`)
shows a clear, replicated collapse in R-hat as `k` grows:

| k | JMbayes2 all-params max R-hat (seed range across replication) |
|---:|---|
| 1  | 1.008 |
| 4  | 1.072 |
| 8  | 191.8 - 329.7 |
| 12 | 6997.6 - 11087.7 |

confirmed consistent across all 3 replication seeds at both k=8 and k=12 (no
seed came close to converging at either point). This is the block-Gibbs
correlation-growth mechanism described in Section 2.4 (Roberts & Sahu 1997):
nothing about the model's identifiability changes with `k` here (the
covariance block is always 2x2), but the *conditional* correlation the
Gibbs step has to move through grows as more absorbable fixed-effects
directions are added to the design - exactly the setting that literature
predicts degrades block/conditional samplers specifically. This is also
precisely why the naive "all-parameters ESS/sec, jmjax vs JMbayes2" ratio
would look enormous at k=12 (hundreds-fold, driven by `J`'s R-hat of
11,000+) without being an honest measurement of anything `jmjax`'s own
reparameterization did - which is the reason this document reports the
regression-only comparison as the trustworthy one, not the larger raw
number.

## 7. Efficiency: real data

### 7.1 AIDS clinical trial data - an independent generalization check

The `aids` dataset bundled with `JMbayes2` (n = 467 patients, CD4 count
over time modeled as `sqrt(CD4) ~ obstime + drug + ...`, `Surv(Time, death)
~ drug`; Guo & Carlin, 2004, *The American Statistician*, 58(1), 16-24) was
deliberately chosen for the real-data check in preference to `pbc2`, for a
reason worth stating explicitly: `pbc2` is the *only* real dataset every
degeneracy diagnostic and every "measured motivation" number quoted in
`jmjax`'s own source code (Section 3.5) has ever touched. A result that only
ever appears on the dataset used to discover it is not yet evidence the
effect generalizes. `aids` is untouched by any of this project's diagnostic
history and is itself a standard, independently-cited benchmark in the
joint-modeling literature (e.g. Rizopoulos, 2010, "JM: An R Package for the
Joint Modelling of Longitudinal and Time-to-Event Data," *Journal of
Statistical Software*, 35(9)), which also makes the result legible to a
reader unfamiliar with this package's own development history.

Across 4 independent seeds (`aids_full.csv`), regression-only ESS/second
ratios against the default fit:

| arm | mean regression-only ESS/sec | mean all-params R-hat | mean regression-only R-hat | per-seed ratio vs A (range) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| A (default) | 23.1 | 1.009 | 1.008 | - |
| D (orth. intercept) | 180.6 | 1.008 | 1.002 | 5.16x - 11.91x |
| E (orth. all) | 209.8 | 1.008 | 1.001 | 5.17x - 13.43x |
| J (JMbayes2, 2 of 4 seeds) | 56.6 | 2.333 | 1.023 | (E vs J: 4.11x, 4.53x, the 2 seeds with a matched J run) |

The pattern replicates the simulated study closely: `jmjax`'s regression
parameters converge cleanly regardless of arm (mean regression-only R-hat
1.001-1.008 across A/D/E), while `JMbayes2`'s all-parameters R-hat is
unstable across seeds (mean 2.33, driven by its covariance block) even
though its own regression-only R-hat (1.023) is reasonable - the same
regression-vs-nuisance split seen throughout this document, now confirmed
on a dataset that played no role in developing any of the diagnostics that
found it.

**The same `alpha`-specific breakdown on real data.** As in the simulated
sweep, pulling `alpha`'s own ESS/sec (also stored per-seed in
`aids_full.csv`, independently of the `min`-based regression-only column)
rather than the composite gives:

| arm | mean alpha ESS/sec | vs A | vs J |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A (default) | 147.2 | - | 2.44x |
| D (orth. intercept) | 206.7 | 1.40x | 3.43x |
| E (orth. all) | 219.2 | 1.49x | 3.64x |
| J (JMbayes2, 2 seeds) | 60.3 | - | - |

`jmjax`'s default fit is already 2.44x faster than `JMbayes2` on `alpha`'s
own mixing, with no reparameterization involved; `orthogonalize_b` adds a
further, real but modest, 1.49x on top (larger than the simulated sweep's
~1.0x for this quantity, though from only 2-4 seeds per arm here - a
difference worth another look, but not one that changes the main
conclusion). Contrast the swept `beta_0`: its own `A`-vs-`E` ESS/sec ratio
on this same dataset is 7.41x - an order of magnitude larger effect,
specific to the coordinate Section 9.1.1's measurement shows is not the one
a user reports.

### 7.2 PBC2

The pre-existing PBC2 benchmark in `vignette("jmjax-validation")`
("Benchmark: jmjax vs JMbayes2" and "Performance tuning") reports a
combined (not orthogonalization-specific) ~4.8x sampling-efficiency
advantage on real, covariate-laden PBC2 data, using the recommended
combination of options documented there. The `orthogonalize_b0`-specific
PBC2 numbers in Section 3.5 (6.6x/>7.6x recoverable ESS on the two affected
coefficients alone) are a different, narrower measurement - the marginal
effect of the location-degeneracy fix specifically, isolated from the other
tuning options in that combined figure. Both are accurately described as
"previously validated," not new results of this document; they are
included here for completeness, and because Section 3.5's numbers are the
direct empirical basis for the mechanism explained in Section 3.

## 8. Mechanism: two architectural layers, not one

A natural reading of the results above is that `jmjax`'s NUTS/HMC sampler is
simply, generally superior to `JMbayes2`'s block sampler - including on
parameters (like `rho`, the random-effects correlation) that no targeted
reparameterization in this package touches at all. That reading is half
right and worth separating into its two actual components, because they
have different degrees of novelty and different literature backing.

### 8.1 Layer 1: generic gradient-based robustness (well-established, not jmjax-specific, and now directly demonstrated)

This layer no longer needs to be inferred indirectly from `rho`'s stability
under growing `k` (though that evidence, kept below, still corroborates
it). Sections 6.3 and 7.1 now report `alpha`'s own ESS/sec, isolated from
any orthogonalization, directly against `JMbayes2`: 5.7x-8.1x in
simulation, 2.44x on real `aids` data, with `orthogonalize_b` contributing
little to nothing further (0.91x-1.15x in simulation; a real but secondary
1.49x on the real dataset). This is exactly the generic NUTS/HMC-vs-block-
Gibbs distinction in Sections 2.2 and 2.4 (Hoffman & Gelman 2014; Roberts &
Sahu 1997; Betancourt 2017): a gradient-based sampler that jointly explores
the full parameter vector via Hamiltonian dynamics has no equivalent of
"conditional on the other blocks' current values," and so has no
equivalent mechanism by which growing inter-parameter correlation
specifically degrades one block's own updates.

The corroborating, indirect evidence: `rho`'s own mixing under `jmjax` is,
on its own terms, unremarkable - its ESS/draw bounces in a narrow band
(roughly 0.06-0.12 across the k-sweep) with no trend as `k` grows, since
neither `orthogonalize_b0` nor `orthogonalize_b` touches `rho` at all. What
is notable is that it is stable rather than degrading - which, given
Section 6.4's finding, is mostly a statement about `JMbayes2` degrading on
its comparable parameter (the covariance block `rho` is derived from), not
about `jmjax` doing anything specifically clever for `rho`.

Taken together, this is real, well-documented, general MCMC theory, now
backed by a direct, reparameterization-free measurement on the parameter
that matters most to a joint-model analysis - not a `jmjax`-specific
architectural achievement, but the part of the comparison that should
carry the paper's headline claim, precisely because it needs no caveat
about which coordinate is being measured.

### 8.2 Layer 2: the targeted reparameterization (a real, verified, but more modest contribution than first measured)

The large, k-independent, highly statistically significant *swept-beta*
advantage (Section 6.3) is real and is not explained by Layer 1 alone -
`beta_1` degrades under the *default* `jmjax` fit too, and orthogonalizing
it removes a genuine, source-verified degeneracy (Section 3), proved not
to change the model (Section 4) and verified so empirically (Section 5).
What Sections 9.1 and 9.1.1 add is that this large effect is specific to
the *swept* coordinate, not to the identified quantity a user reports:
measured on `beta_corrected`, the reportable estimand, the gain is a
pilot-measured 1.25x-1.31x (Section 9.1.1), not 13x-15x. The option's
honest efficiency contribution is therefore modest - closer in size to
Layer 1's own secondary effect on `alpha` (Section 7.1's 1.49x) than to
the headline number this document originally reported for it. Its more
durable contribution is the one Section 9.1 documents at length:
diagnosing and correcting a real posterior-calibration bug that silently
miscalibrates credible intervals for swept coefficients, in exactly the
way an earlier, retracted attempt at the same problem did. A follow-up
construction (Section 9.1.2), not yet validated to the same standard as
the rest of this document, suggests the 1.25x-1.31x figure above is not
the end of the story - see that section before treating it as a ceiling.

### 8.3 Synthesis

The evidence now supports a different apportionment than the first draft's:
the large, robust, statistically significant, twice-replicated (simulated
and real-data) advantage over `JMbayes2` on the parameter a joint-model
analysis is usually run to estimate - `alpha` - is Layer 1, present in
`jmjax`'s default fit with no option enabled, and is well-established,
generic HMC/NUTS-vs-block-Gibbs theory rather than a novel architectural
claim of this package. `orthogonalize_b0`/`orthogonalize_b` (Layer 2) is a
genuine, source-verified, formally proved fix for a real identifiability
bug that recurs for any random slope on time - worth reporting on its own,
narrower terms - but its own efficiency contribution, honestly measured on
the coordinates it is safe to report, is modest, not the order-of-magnitude
figure it appeared to be before Section 9.1.1's measurement. Framed this
way, the claim that `jmjax` reflects "elegant parameterization and problem
formulation" is well supported for the calibration-bug diagnosis and fix
specifically; the claim that it explains most of `jmjax`'s speed advantage
over `JMbayes2` is not, and should not be made in the paper's headline.

## 9. Limitations and open questions

### 9.1 Posterior calibration: a negative result, and its correction

The first draft of this document listed posterior calibration as the
single most important unchecked item, with no evidence either way. It has
now been checked (`dev/study_calibration.R`), and the answer for the
reported parameterization is negative.

The study simulates $R$ replicates at $N = 300$, fits each under three
arms - **A** (unmodified), **D** (`orthogonalize_b0`), **E**
(`orthogonalize_b`) - and reports, per arm and estimand, coverage of the
central credible intervals together with
$\mathrm{sd\_ratio} = \overline{\mathrm{SD}(\beta \mid y)} \big/
\mathrm{SD}\big(\mathbb{E}[\beta \mid y]\big)$, the average posterior SD
divided by the across-replicate spread of the posterior means. A
calibrated posterior reports, on average, the spread its point estimates
actually have, so $\mathrm{sd\_ratio}$ sits at 1; below 1 means intervals
too narrow. It is a far sharper instrument than coverage at any
affordable replicate count, because it uses the whole interval rather
than a binary hit - and it is the exact shape of the
`wishart_gibbs_centered` failure.

At $R = 100$ replicates on the `linear` design, $N = 300$, 500 warmup +
1000 draws over 2 chains, gated at regression-only
$\widehat{R} \le 1.05$ (95% coverage carries a Monte Carlo SE of about
$0.011$ at this count):

| estimand | arm A | arm D | arm E |
|---|---|---|---|
| `beta_0` sd_ratio | 1.164 | **0.262** | **0.264** |
| `beta_0` cov95 | 0.990 | **0.323** | **0.320** |
| `beta_slope` sd_ratio | 1.027 | 1.032 | **0.223** |
| `beta_slope` cov95 | 0.970 | 0.960 | **0.250** |
| `alpha` sd_ratio | 0.922 | 0.920 | 0.921 |
| `alpha` cov95 | 0.930 | 0.929 | 0.920 |
| `sigma_b0` sd_ratio | 0.914 | 0.906 | 0.910 |

Put in absolute terms, against the across-replicate spread of the
posterior means - the quantity a calibrated posterior SD should be
estimating:

| | empirical SD | mean posterior SD | intervals too narrow by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `beta_0`, arm A | 0.0587 | 0.0660 | - (1.16x, mildly conservative) |
| `beta_0`, arm D / E | 0.0587 | **0.0154** | **3.8x** |
| `beta_slope`, arm A / D | 0.0172 | 0.0178 | - (1.03x) |
| `beta_slope`, arm E | 0.0172 | **0.0038** | **4.5x** |

Point estimates are unbiased throughout: the largest relative bias in any
arm or estimand among $\beta_0$, $\beta_{\text{slope}}$ and
$\sigma_{b_0}$ is $0.5\%$.

The pattern is a clean dose-response and leaves little room for an
alternative reading. Arm D sweeps only the intercept column and damages
only `beta_0`; arm E sweeps both and damages both; `beta_slope` under D is
untouched, as it must be, since D never touches that column. The
unmodified fit is itself well calibrated on `beta_slope` (1.027) and
mildly conservative on `beta_0` (1.164), so arm A rather than nominal
$0.95$ is the target a correction should be matching.

`alpha` is carried deliberately as a **negative control**: it lives in the
survival submodel and never meets the subject-constant column space, so no
arm should move it. None does - and the agreement is far tighter than the
table can show. Paired replicate by replicate, the mean difference in
`alpha`'s posterior mean is $+2 \times 10^{-5}$ between arms D and A and
$+1 \times 10^{-4}$ between E and A, i.e. $0.04\%$ and $0.2\%$ of a single
posterior standard deviation. `sigma_b0` behaves the same way, which also
settles an open question posed in `mcmc_model.py`'s own source comment:
sweeping does **not** shift `sigma_b0`'s posterior.

That the damage is invisible to a point-estimate check is the whole
difficulty. It is exactly why `wishart_gibbs_centered` survived inspection
for as long as it did, and exactly why this study reports interval width
rather than agreement of means.

**The correction restores calibration.** Applying $\tilde\beta$ of
Section 4.9 - post-processing each arm's own draws, with no refit - at
$R = 16$ replicates under the same settings (the 100-replicate
confirmation is in progress):

| estimand | arm A | arm D | arm E | D corrected | E corrected |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `beta_0` sd_ratio | 1.177 | 0.283 | 0.283 | **1.181** | **1.193** |
| `beta_slope` sd_ratio | 1.184 | 1.183 | 0.267 | **1.183** | **1.195** |

with 95% coverage restored to $1.00$ in every corrected cell. The
agreement is stronger than the table shows, because it holds **per
replicate** and not merely in aggregate: arm D's corrected `beta_0` tracks
arm A's `beta_0` across replicates at $r = 0.9999$, with a mean absolute
gap of $0.0007$ against $0.0082$ for the uncorrected comparison - an order
of magnitude tighter. That is the signature Proposition 6 predicts, since
the correction reconstructs what the unmodified parameterization would
have reported *given the same* `b_raw` draw, rather than merely landing on
a similar variance.

The practical reading, pending the larger run: `beta` from an
orthogonalized fit is a *constrained* estimand and its interval should not
be reported for a swept parameter; `beta_corrected` is the identified one
and is what a user should report. The sampler still works in the
well-conditioned geometry - that is the entire point - and the reporting
is done in the identified coordinates afterwards.

### 9.1.1 A second negative result: the correction's own effective sample size

Restoring calibration is not the same as restoring efficiency, and this
mattered enough to check before the corrected estimand's efficiency was
assumed rather than measured. `dev/pilot_ess_corrected.R` computes
`beta_corrected`'s own R-hat/ESS via the package's own estimator
(`recompute_site_diagnostics()`, the same routine `jm_fit()` uses for the
standardize_covariates back-transform), applied post hoc to an
orthogonalized fit's stored draws - no backend change, no refit.

At 2 seeds (`n = 300`, 500 warmup + 1000 samples x 2 chains, the `linear`
design), `E vs A` ESS/sec:

| parameter | `beta` (swept) | `beta_corrected` (reportable) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `beta_0` | 9.08x-9.11x | 1.25x-1.29x |
| `beta_slope` | 15.02x | 1.28x-1.31x |

The swept coordinate's own gain replicates the k-sweep and `aids` findings
closely (Sections 6.3, 7.1); the reportable estimand's does not. This
document had earlier predicted the opposite here - that `beta_corrected`
would mix close to `beta`'s own rate, because the swept component "is
unconstrained by the likelihood and therefore mixes at essentially the
prior's rate." That prediction is falsified by this measurement, and the
reason is instructive rather than merely disappointing.

**Why the prediction failed.** Section 2.7 (Geyer, 1992) is the general
point: ESS belongs to a specific scalar functional of the chain, not to
"the sampler." The sampled `beta` in an orthogonalized fit is $\beta$
in Section 4.9's notation, and `beta_corrected` is $\tilde\beta$, obtained
by applying $\Phi$ to the stored draws - a different linear functional of
$(\beta, b_{\mathrm{raw}})$ than $\beta$ alone, with no general guarantee
of inheriting its mixing rate. (An earlier version of this paragraph used
the two symbols the other way round.) The specific mechanism: the location
degeneracy this document diagnoses was always a trade-off, in the
unconstrained model, between its coefficient - $\tilde\beta$ - and the
linear combination $Q^{\top}b_{\mathrm{raw}}[\cdot, q_\ast]$ that
Proposition 6 subtracts. Sampling in the orthogonalized parameterization
and recovering $\tilde\beta$ afterwards does not remove that trade-off
($\Phi$ has unit Jacobian and preserves the likelihood; Proposition 6(i)-(iii) show it cannot), it
*relocates* which coordinate carries it: the sampled $\beta$ becomes the
well-identified combination (fast-mixing, as Sections 6.3/7.1
confirm), and the degeneracy is now expressed entirely through
$Q^{\top}b_{\mathrm{raw}}[\cdot, q_\ast]$ - the very quantity the recovery
step adds back in. That quantity is not an isolated, prior-dominated
scalar the way this document's original hypothesis assumed; it lives
inside a hierarchical random-effects block with its own, separate,
already-documented curvature pathology (Neal's funnel, correctly
distinguished from this document's location problem in Section 2.2),
governed by `sigma_b`/`L_corr` and by the single global step size and mass
matrix NUTS must use across every direction in `b` simultaneously.
`orthogonalize_b`/`_b0` was designed against the location problem, not
against the b-block's own internal conditioning, so the relocated
direction inherits whatever mixing rate that block already had - which
this measurement puts close to a default fit's, not close to the prior's.

**Correction (Section 4.10).** The mechanism proposed in the paragraph
above - that the relocated direction inherits the `b` block's funnel-type
conditioning under `sigma_b` - is not needed to explain this measurement,
and is kept only as a record of what was believed when it was made.
Section 4.10 shows, in a closed-form check with every variance component
held fixed (so no funnel can arise), that misalignment is sufficient: the
generator coordinate $u = Q_0^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}[\cdot, 0]$ that the
correction adds back is dominated by an exactly flat component (all of it
when $\rho = 0$) with unit variance given the variance components, lying
oblique to the per-subject coordinates, so a diagonal mass matrix cannot
rescale it; its whitened variance grows with the information each subject
carries about its own random effects (Proposition 10(a)). Whether the
funnel adds to this once the variance components are sampled is not
settled by that check. The first half of the paragraph - that ESS belongs
to the functional, and that the correction relocates the trade-off rather
than removing it - stands.

**What this does and does not affect.** It changes the efficiency claim
for the swept coefficients specifically: `beta`'s large ESS/sec gain is
real but not reportable, and `beta_corrected`'s reportable gain is modest.
It does not touch `alpha`, `gamma`, or any parameter outside the swept
subspace - `alpha`'s own ESS/sec advantage over `JMbayes2` (Sections 6.3,
7.1) is a different functional entirely, unaffected by any of this
machinery, which is exactly why it survives as the paper's central claim
(Section 8).

**Caveat.** This is a 2-seed pilot for one design (`linear`, `N = 300`).
The direction is corroborated independently - the `aids` table's own
`beta_0` numbers (Section 7.1) reproduce a comparable `E`-vs-`A` figure to
the one this pilot finds for the swept coordinate - which is reassuring
about the machinery, but the exact 1.25x-1.31x figure for
`beta_corrected` should be treated as a preliminary estimate, not a final
number, until more seeds are run.

### 9.1.2 A follow-up: isolating the relocated degeneracy recovers most of the missing efficiency

Section 9.1.1 traced the corrected estimand's disappointing ESS/sec to a
specific mechanism: the relocated degeneracy lands inside `b_std[:, 0]`, a
several-hundred-dimensional per-subject block, and inherits whatever
mixing rate NUTS's single global mass matrix gives that block as a whole -
not the near-prior rate this document's original hypothesis assumed. That
diagnosis suggests a fix: give the specific direction the degeneracy
occupies its own, small, separately-adapted coordinate, rather than
leaving it buried inside a large block tuned for everything else in it.

**The construction.** `b_raw[:, 0] = sigma_b[0] * b_std[:, 0]` always - a
valid Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix has first row
$[1, 0, \ldots, 0]$ - so `b_std[:, 0]` can be split, with no
approximation, into a component along the orthonormal basis $Q$ that
`orthogonalize_b0`/`orthogonalize_b` already computes (the absorbable
directions) and a component along its orthogonal complement $Q_\perp$:
`b_std[:, 0]` $= Qu + Q_\perp v$, with $u$, $v$ independent standard
normal of dimension $k$ (typically 1-4) and $N_{\mathrm{sub}} - k$
respectively. Because this is a rotation of a spherical Gaussian, it is
exact: `b_std[:, 0]` marginally, and jointly with every other parameter,
has precisely the same distribution as before, and
$u = Q^{\top}$`b_std[:, 0]` recovers exactly the generator coordinate the
degeneracy lives in (verified in pure NumPy to machine precision,
independently of the model). $u$ is then sampled as its own, explicitly
small NUTS site (`control$orthogonalize_b0_rotate = TRUE`), optionally
given its own dense mass-matrix block via NumPyro's existing
block-diagonal mechanism (`control$dense_mass_b0_generator = TRUE`) - the
same mechanism `dense_mass_beta`/`dense_mass_spline` already use elsewhere
in this package. No other part of the model changes: the sweep, the
survival submodel, and the `beta_corrected` post-processing of Section 4.9
read `b_std`/`L_corr`/`sigma_b` exactly as before and do not know whether
`b_std` was rotated. The construction is currently scoped to the
intercept column only - the slope column's analogous direction depends on
the sampled correlation $\rho$, so a fixed, precomputed rotation cannot
isolate it the same way. Section 4.10 (Lemma 1, Corollary 4) shows that this obstacle is
avoidable: rotating every column by the same fixed basis contains the
$\rho$-dependent direction inside a small explicit block for every value
of $\rho$.

**Efficiency.** `beta_corrected`'s own ESS/sec, relative to a default
fit's `beta_0` (the closest available like-for-like reference, since a
default fit never reports a corrected estimand):

| pilot | baseline hazard | seeds | `orthogonalize_b0` alone | `+ orthogonalize_b0_rotate` | `+ dense_mass_b0_generator` |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | spline | 2 | 0.91x | 7.61x | 5.23x |
| 2 | spline | 6 | 0.93x | 5.77x | 5.81x |
| 3 | weibull | 2 | 1.05x | 6.52x | 5.64x |

(all three on the `linear` design, `N = 300`). The rotation alone
recovers most of the gap between the plain option's 1.25x-1.31x
(Section 9.1.1) and the swept, unreportable coordinate's own 9x-15x,
consistently across two baseline-hazard forms and both seed counts tried.
The additional dense mass-matrix block does not reliably help on top of
the rotation - it trails it in two of three pilots and ties it in the
third - unlike the rotation itself, which improved on the plain option in
every pilot run. Section 4.10 predicts this: once $u$ is its own coordinate, what remains
slow lies along the slope column's generator coordinate, which a dense
block on $u$ alone cannot reach (Corollary 3(i), Proposition 10(b)). A correctness check accompanies every pilot:
`beta_corrected`'s posterior mean agrees between the rotated and
unrotated fit at the same seed to within Monte Carlo noise (mean absolute
difference $0.0009$-$0.0018$ across the three pilots, against posterior
means of order $2$), consistent with the rotation being exact rather than
merely well-behaved.

**Calibration.** An exact reparameterization of the sampling coordinates
cannot change the target posterior, but "provably exact" and "confirmed
by this document's own calibration instrument" are different claims - and
the instrument exists precisely because an earlier reparameterization
(`wishart_gibbs_centered`) was likelihood-invariant and unbiased
throughout, and was retracted only because its intervals turned out too
narrow (Section 9.1). `dev/study_calibration.R` was extended with a
`D_rot` arm (`orthogonalize_b0` + `orthogonalize_b0_rotate`) and run at
$R = 100$ on the `linear` design, gated identically to Section 9.1:

| estimand | arm A (`beta_0`, plain - A is never orthogonalized) | arm D `beta_0_corrected` | arm D_rot `beta_0_corrected` |
|---|---|---|---|
| cov95 | 0.990 | 0.990 | 0.990 |
| sd_ratio | 1.164 | 1.164 | 1.156 |
| bias/se | 1.68 | 1.52 | 1.55 |
| `alpha` cov95 (negative control) | 0.930 | 0.929 | 0.930 |

Arm A's row is its own plain `beta_0` - the target a correction should be
matching, per Section 9.1 - not a corrected quantity, since nothing is
swept for an unmodified fit. `D_rot`'s coverage matches `D`'s exactly and
its sd_ratio differs by
$0.008$ - noise at this replicate count (Monte Carlo SE on 95% coverage is
about $0.011$ here), nowhere near the fourfold narrowing
`wishart_gibbs_centered` produced. The negative control does not move
either. Proposition 8 (Section 4.10) has since shown the equality is exact,
so this comparison is best read as a check that the implementation is
correct, not as evidence about the construction. This is also, incidentally, the $R = 100$ confirmation Section 9.1
flagged as "in progress" for arm D's own correction: the plain option's
calibration fix is now confirmed at full replicate count, not only the
$R = 16$ pilot reported there; arm E's equivalent confirmation remains
open.

**Status.** This is a promising, internally consistent result, but it
should not be read as validated to the standard the rest of this document
uses. It has been checked on one design (`linear`), one baseline hazard
beyond the initial spline pilot (Weibull), a handful of seeds per
configuration (not the covariate-count sweep of Section 6 or the
independent real-data check of Section 7), and only for the intercept
column (`orthogonalize_b0`, not `orthogonalize_b`'s slope sweep). It is
also new code, implemented and reviewed but not traced by its authoring
session (no JAX/NumPyro environment was available during implementation -
see `dev/pilot_b0_rotate.R`'s header), so its first executions are the
ones reported here rather than the product of independent pre-release
testing. It ships as two opt-in `control` arguments, off by default,
alongside the existing `orthogonalize_b0`/`orthogonalize_b` options; it
does not change either option's own behaviour when left at its default
(`FALSE`). A known interaction: a warm-started fit's initial value for
`b_std` is silently not applied to the rotated columns, since `b_std`
becomes a derived quantity rather than a sampled one under the rotation
(a soft degradation - NUTS still starts from a valid point - not a
correctness issue). Section 9.3 lists what remains before this could be
reported with the same confidence as Sections 6-8.

### 9.2 Remaining limitations

- **An unrelated finding the same study surfaced, recorded here rather than
  dropped.** The negative control `alpha` is arm-invariant to a remarkable
  degree, which is what it was included to check. But in *every* arm,
  including the unmodified fit, its posterior mean sits about $2.8\%$ above
  the truth ($0.5142$ against $0.500$) - $32\%$ of one posterior standard
  deviation, or $2.97$ Monte Carlo standard errors at $R = 100$ - with
  $\mathrm{sd\_ratio}$ $0.92$ and 95% coverage $0.93$. `sigma_b0` shows a
  milder version of the same pattern ($\mathrm{sd\_ratio}$ $0.91$, coverage
  $0.94$, bias $0.3\%$). Because the effect is identical across arms it
  says nothing whatever about the reparameterization, which is the claim
  this document makes; it is a property of the joint model, this
  simulation design, or this sample size, and it appeared only because
  this is the first time these fits were replicated 100 times and examined
  for *coverage* rather than point agreement. It is reported because a
  coverage table that includes a negative control should show what the
  negative control actually did: omitting `alpha` once it showed something
  would undermine the value of having included it. Diagnosing it - finite-
  sample bias in the association parameter is a plausible and
  well-precedented candidate - is separate work, and it should be
  understood before this table is put in front of a referee.
- **The reparameterization's own efficiency contribution, once correctly
  measured, is modest as shipped.** Section 9.1.1: a 2-seed pilot puts
  `beta_corrected`'s ESS/sec gain over a default fit at roughly
  1.25x-1.31x, not the 9x-15x measured for the swept, unreportable `beta`.
  This does not undermine the calibration fix itself (Section 9.1) or the
  option's value as a bug fix, but it does mean the option should not be
  marketed on efficiency grounds alone; Section 8 gives the reattributed
  picture, with `alpha`'s own advantage over `JMbayes2` (Sections 6.3, 7.1)
  now carrying the paper's central efficiency claim instead. A follow-up
  construction (Section 9.1.2) recovers most of this gap in pilot testing
  while preserving calibration, but is not yet validated broadly enough
  to revise this bullet's headline number for the package as shipped.
- The option currently requires `q >= 2`, `random_effects_corr = TRUE`, and
  `random_effects_method = "nuts"` (the default); other combinations raise
  an informative error rather than silently no-op'ing, but the option's
  coverage of `jmjax`'s other random-effects code paths (e.g.
  `wishart_gibbs`, uncorrelated random effects) is simply untested, not
  ruled out.
- It remains an opt-in, experimental option, not the default.
- The sample-size (`n`) dimension of this study is incomplete: only `n =
  500` at `k in {1, 3}` was run before the covariate-count question took
  priority (per an explicit, deliberate scope decision - see project
  history); a proper `n`-scaling characterization, orthogonal to the
  `k`-sweep reported here, remains open.
- **The completeness gap is closed** (was: "`_absorbable_basis` is sound
  but not complete"). Section 4 supplies the formal treatment, and the
  result is two-sided. Soundness always held: every direction removed is
  genuinely absorbable by `beta` (Propositions 2 and 3), so Corollary 1's
  model-invariance claim - which underwrites every number in Sections 5
  to 8 - is established rather than assumed. Completeness did *not* hold
  for the column-wise search (Proposition 4 and Example 1), and the
  failure was silent: with a spline or orthogonal-polynomial longitudinal
  mean plus a random slope, the dominant degeneracy was left untreated
  while the intercept column still produced a basis, so no warning fired.
  The basis-independent null-space construction of Section 4.5 now ships
  as `_absorbable_basis_exact()` and is authoritative (Section 4.8). What
  remains open is narrower: behaviour under *near*-collinearity, where the
  rank decision is a tolerance judgement rather than a clean split.
- **Condition (S) is checked, not argued.** `_structural_extension_residual()`
  evaluates the proportionality on the event and quadrature grids at every
  fit and warns when it fails (Section 4.8). The residual is reported, so
  a design that satisfies the grid test by coincidence is now visible
  rather than silently accepted.
- The simulation design here uses a Weibull survival submodel and a
  specific covariate structure (three named covariates plus independent
  Gaussian extras). Generalization to the spline-baseline hazard, to
  covariates with their own structure (e.g. correlated covariates, or
  covariate-by-time interactions, which `_absorbable_basis`'s own docstring
  notes it would also pick up), and to designs without a random slope at
  all, is plausible by construction but not separately re-verified by the
  study in this document.

### 9.3 Next validation steps, in priority order

1. **Implement Corollary 4, then test Section 4.10's predictions by
   simulation.** Section 4.10 proves the rotation exact and predicts when,
   and by roughly how much, it helps, which turns "broader validation"
   into specific checks that could fail. In order: (a) implement the
   all-column rotation with a Householder completion as a new opt-in
   setting alongside the current one, so the two can be compared on the
   same seeds, including under `orthogonalize_b`; (b) a pilot grid
   crossing visits per subject (sparse against dense follow-up),
   $\sigma_e$, and the generating $\rho \in \{0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9\}$,
   recording `beta_corrected` ESS/sec for both the intercept and the slope
   and checking the three predictions stated under Section 4.10's table
   (the current rotation's dependence on $\rho$, the slope's
   recovery under the all-column rotation, and invariance in
   $N \in \{150, 300, 600\}$), together with per-fit wall time and tree
   depth, since overhead is the one thing the theory does not predict;
   (c) the $R = 100$ calibration study for the new arm on the `linear`
   and `mixing` designs - Proposition 8 predicts equality, so this checks
   the implementation; (d) the real-data check of Section 7 (`aids`,
   PBC2); and (e) resolving the warm-start interaction noted in Section
   9.1.2's "Status" paragraph. Only after (b)-(d) would there be grounds
   to consider the rotation - together with `orthogonalize_b0`/`_b` and
   reporting `beta_corrected` as the primary estimand - as a default, a
   user-facing change that would need its own discussion.
2. **More seeds for the plain correction's effective sample size -
   corroborated, not yet closed.** Section 9.1.1's 2-seed figure
   (1.25x-1.31x) has since been corroborated by two further pilots at 6
   spline seeds and 2 Weibull seeds (Section 9.1.2's table; the plain-
   option column there reads 0.91x-1.05x, consistent pilot-to-pilot noise
   around the same modest figure). Computing the correction on by-chain
   draws directly, rather than post hoc via `recompute_site_diagnostics()`
   on pooled draws, remains open.
3. **The prior-weight diagnostic of Proposition 7.** $w$ is computable draw
   by draw from quantities already stored; reporting
   $\mathrm{ESS}(\{w\})$, or simply $\mathrm{sd}(\log w)$, converts
   Corollary 2's asymptotic argument into a per-fit check and would make
   the correction self-validating on designs and priors not covered here.
4. **The 100-replicate calibration run, extended to arm E and the
   `mixing` design.** Arm D's correction is now confirmed at $R = 100$ on
   the `linear` design (Section 9.1.2); arm E's remains at the original
   $R = 16$ pilot scale, and the `mixing` design - where the per-column
   search finds *nothing* for the slope column, exercising the full
   sequence of defect, repair, and correction in one arm - has not yet
   been run at either scale. Condition (S) has been verified to hold
   there ($3 \times 10^{-16}$), so the correction is applicable.
5. **Coverage of the other random-effects code paths**, per the second
   bullet of Section 9.2.

## 10. Related work summary

Section 2 covers this in full; in brief, this document sits at the
intersection of (a) general non-centered/centered reparameterization theory
for hierarchical models (Papaspiliopoulos & Roberts 2003; Papaspiliopoulos,
Roberts & Sköld 2007), (b) the specific geometric account of why this
matters for Hamiltonian/NUTS samplers (Betancourt & Girolami 2013;
Betancourt 2017; Hoffman & Gelman 2014; Neal 2003 for the related-but-
distinct funnel case), (c) the complementary account of why block/Gibbs
samplers are specifically vulnerable to the resulting growing correlation
(Roberts & Sahu 1997), (d) applied precedent for this failure mode in
hierarchical Bayesian models generally (Ogle et al. 2020), and (e) the
classical fact that effective sample size is a property of the specific
functional of the chain being monitored rather than of the sampler itself
(Geyer 1992) - needed in Section 9.1.1 to explain why the swept coordinate
and the identified estimand recovered from it can, and here do, have very
different effective sample sizes. Two further literatures turned out to bear directly on the correction
and its efficiency: restricted spatial regression (Reich, Hodges & Zadnik 2006; Hughes & Haran 2013;
Hanks et al. 2015; Khan & Calder 2022; Bradley 2024), whose
back-transformation Section 4.9 generalizes to joint models, and the
analysis of linear preconditioning for HMC (Neal 2011; Hird & Livingstone
2025), on which Section 4.10's account of the rotation rests, together
with the standard characterization of non-identified parameters (Dawid
1979; Poirier 1998; Gustafson 2015). Its contribution is the specific
diagnosis, source-verified mechanism, and replicated empirical
characterization of the location-degeneracy problem for joint
longitudinal-survival models; the finding, on direct measurement, that
`jmjax`'s efficiency advantage over `JMbayes2` on the parameters a user
actually reports is predominantly a generic HMC/NUTS-vs-block-Gibbs effect
(Section 8) rather than a product of this reparameterization; and a
correction, proved exact, that restores calibration for the swept
coefficients this document's fix affects.

## 11. Conclusion

`jmjax`'s efficiency advantage over `JMbayes2` is real, large, statistically
significant, and replicated across simulated and (for the `aids` dataset)
genuinely independent real data - but it belongs mainly to `jmjax`'s
generic NUTS/HMC engine, not to the reparameterization this document set
out to validate. Measured directly and without any option enabled, a
default `jmjax` fit already beats `JMbayes2` on `alpha`'s own ESS/second -
the association parameter a joint-model analysis is usually run to
estimate - by 5.7x-8.1x in simulation and 2.44x on real data (Sections 6.3,
7.1). This is well-documented, general sampler-class theory (gradient-based
HMC/NUTS versus block-Gibbs/Metropolis, Section 8.1), demonstrated here
rather than only argued for, and it is the claim this paper should lead
with.

`orthogonalize_b0`/`orthogonalize_b` remains a genuine, worthwhile
contribution, but on narrower terms than first drafted. The
reparameterization diagnoses and fixes a real identifiability problem - a
location degeneracy between subject-constant fixed effects and matching
random effects, that recurs independently of covariate count for any
random slope on time - down to the level of source code, and proves the
fix does not change the model (Section 4). It also uncovers, and repairs,
a real posterior-calibration bug: the swept coordinates it reports come
back miscalibrated, exactly as an earlier, retracted attempt at the same
problem was, and the correction of Section 4.9 restores both coverage and
interval width in closed form, with no refit. What it does *not* deliver,
on the evidence in Section 9.1.1, is a large efficiency gain for the
coefficients it targets, once measured on the coordinates a user may
actually report: a pilot puts that gain at roughly 1.25x-1.31x, an order
of magnitude short of the swept coordinate's own, unreportable 9x-15x. The
option is best described, honestly, as a correctness fix with a modest
efficiency side benefit, not as an efficiency feature.

The calibration question the first draft named as the blocker has been
answered, and answering it is what surfaced the ESS question that, in
turn, changed this document's central claim. Both findings share the same
shape: a reparameterization can make a chosen coordinate look excellent -
unbiased and fast-mixing - while the quantity a user actually needs is a
different functional of the same draws, subject to no such guarantee
(Section 2.7). The practical upshot for this package is a clean division
of labor: report `alpha`, `gamma`, and other unswept parameters from a
default fit and credit the sampler; use
`orthogonalize_b0`/`orthogonalize_b` when a swept coefficient's calibration
matters, report `beta_corrected` rather than `beta`, and expect a modest,
not dramatic, efficiency dividend for doing so.

A late addition complicates that last clause without overturning it: a
follow-up construction (`orthogonalize_b0_rotate`, Section 9.1.2) recovers
most of the missing efficiency for the intercept-swept coefficient in
every pilot run so far - roughly 5x-8x over a default fit, against the
1.25x-1.31x above - while leaving calibration unchanged within noise on
the one design checked ($R = 100$). It is reported here because the
evidence is consistent, not because it has earned the same confidence as
the rest of this document: it needs the breadth of validation Section 9.3
lists (more designs, real data, the slope column, more calibration
replicates) before "modest, not dramatic" above should be revised for the
package as shipped. Until then, the honest summary is: the correctness
fix is proven and ships; a further efficiency fix on top of it looks
promising in early testing but is not yet ready to promise. Section 4.10 has since narrowed what "not yet" means: the construction
is proven exact, so what remains open is how much it helps and at what
cost - questions the theory now answers in advance of the simulations that
must confirm it.

## 12. Note on publication venue

For the record, and as requested: this material is suited to a package
vignette regardless of any further venue (this document); beyond that, the
combination of a general, citable methodological contribution (Sections 2-
3, 8-9) with a software package it ships in and validates (Sections 5-7)
fits the scope of the *Journal of Statistical Software* or *The R Journal*
best (both have precedent for exactly this pairing - `JMbayes2` itself was
introduced this way). A parallel arXiv preprint (`stat.CO` or `stat.ME`) is
low-cost and would establish priority independently of review timelines.
`Bayesian Analysis`, `Statistics in Medicine`, and `Computational Statistics
& Data Analysis` are reasonable alternates if a narrower statistical-
methodology framing (rather than software-paper framing) is preferred.
Section 9's calibration gap, which an earlier draft flagged as the blocker
here, is now closed in both directions: the negative result is measured and
the correction is proved and validated (Sections 4.9 and 9.1). That
strengthens rather than weakens the submission - a reviewer in this area
would have asked for the coverage study, and the honest answer now comes
with a remedy attached rather than a caveat. Following that check to its
conclusion also moved the paper's own headline (Sections 8, 9.1.1, 11): the
efficiency claim a reviewer should be shown first is now `alpha`'s
reparameterization-independent advantage over `JMbayes2` (real and large on
two datasets), not the reparameterization's own effect on swept
coefficients (real but modest once measured on `beta_corrected`). The
remaining items worth having in hand before submission are the broader
validation of the rotation follow-up (Section 9.1.2; Section 9.3, item 1)
if it is to be included as a package feature rather than a documented
pilot result, and, more modestly, a few more seeds of the plain
correction's ESS pilot (Section 9.3, item 2) to firm up the 1.25x-1.31x
figure - neither changes the paper's central claim (Section 8), which
rests on `alpha`'s reparameterization-independent advantage rather than on
either of these items.
